entries.aa0ab4545eb9f2813530e69437fb29df1505bee7: <div sID="gen19489" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Dan.7" sID="Dan.7"/> <div eID="gen19489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19490" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19491" type="x-p"/> The six former chapters of this book were historical; we now enter with fear and trembling upon the six latter, which are prophetical, wherein are many things dark and hard to be understood, which we dare not positively determine the sense of, and yet many things plain and profitable, which I trust God will enable us to make a good use of. In this chapter we have, I. Daniel's vision of the four beasts, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.1-Dan.7.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. His vision of God's throne of government and judgment, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.9-Dan.7.14">ver. 9-14</reference>. III. The interpretation of these visions, given him by an angel that stood by, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.15-Dan.7.28">ver. 15-28</reference>. Whether those visions look as far forward as the end of time, or whether they were to have a speedy accomplishment, is hard to say, nor are the most judicious interpreters agreed concerning it.
entries.054642b3529a332dde8df71f35e8e03dc33ad0b0: <div eID="gen19491" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19490" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Four Beasts. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 555.)</title> <div sID="gen19492" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon Daniel had a dream and visions of his head upon his bed: then he wrote the dream, <hi type="italic">and</hi> told the sum of the matters. <hi type="super">2</hi> Daniel spake and said, I saw in my vision by night, and, behold, the four winds of the heaven strove upon the great sea. <hi type="super">3</hi> And four great beasts came up from the sea, diverse one from another. <hi type="super">4</hi> The first <hi type="italic">was</hi> like a lion, and had eagle's wings: I beheld till the wings thereof were plucked, and it was lifted up from the earth, and made stand upon the feet as a man, and a man's heart was given to it. <hi type="super">5</hi> And behold another beast, a second, like to a bear, and it raised up itself on one side, and <hi type="italic">it had</hi> three ribs in the mouth of it between the teeth of it: and they said thus unto it, Arise, devour much flesh. <hi type="super">6</hi> After this I beheld, and lo another, like a leopard, which had upon the back of it four wings of a fowl; the beast had also four heads; and dominion was given to it. <hi type="super">7</hi> After this I saw in the night visions, and behold a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth: it devoured and brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with the feet of it: and it <hi type="italic">was</hi> diverse from all the beasts that <hi type="italic">were</hi> before it; and it had ten horns. <hi type="super">8</hi> I considered the horns, and, behold, there came up among them another little horn, before whom there were three of the first horns plucked up by the roots: and, behold, in this horn <hi type="italic">were</hi> eyes like the eyes of man, and a mouth speaking great things. <div eID="gen19492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19493" type="x-p"/> The date of this chapter places it before <reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.31">ch. v.</reference>, which was in the last year of Belshazzar, and <reference osisRef="Dan.6.1-Dan.6.28">ch. iv.</reference>, which was in the first of Darius; for Daniel had those visions in the first year of Belshazzar, when the captivity of the Jews in Babylon was drawing near a period. Belshazzar's name here is, in the original, spelt differently from what it used to be; before it was <hi type="italic">Bel-she-azar—Bel is he that treasures up riches.</hi> But this is <hi type="italic">Bel-eshe-zar—Bel is on fire by the enemy.</hi> Bel was the god of the Chaldeans; he had prospered, but is now to be consumed. <div eID="gen19493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19494" type="x-p"/> We have, in these verses, Daniel's vision of the four monarchies that were oppressive to the Jews. Observe, <div eID="gen19494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19495" type="x-p"/> I. The circumstances of this vision. Daniel had interpreted Nebuchadnezzar's dream, and now he is himself honoured with similar divine discoveries (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.1">v. 1</reference>): He <hi type="italic">had visions of his head upon his bed,</hi> when he was asleep; so God sometimes revealed himself and his mind to the children of men, when deep sleep fell upon them (<reference osisRef="Job.33.15">Job xxxiii. 15</reference>); for when we are most retired from the world, and taken off from the things of sense, we are most fit for communion with God. But when he was awake he <hi type="italic">wrote the dream</hi> for his own use, lest he should forget it as a dream which passes away; and he <hi type="italic">told the sum of the matters</hi> to his brethren the Jews for their use, and gave it to them in writing, that it might be communicated to those at a distance and preserved for their children after them, who shall see these things accomplished. The Jews, misunderstanding some of the prophecies of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, flattered themselves with hopes that, after their return to their own land, they should enjoy a complete and uninterrupted tranquility; but that they might not so deceive themselves, and their calamities be made doubly grievous by the disappointment, God by this prophet lets them know that they shall have tribulation: those promises of their prosperity were to be accomplished in the spiritual blessings of the kingdom of grace; as Christ has told his disciples they must expect persecution, and the promises they depend upon will be accomplished in the eternal blessings of the kingdom of glory. Daniel both wrote these things and spoke them, to intimate that the church should be taught both by the scriptures and by ministers' preaching, both by the written word and by word of mouth; and ministers in their preaching are to <hi type="italic">tell the sum of the matters</hi> that are written. <div eID="gen19495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19496" type="x-p"/> II. The vision itself, which foretels the revolutions of government in those nations which the church of the Jews, for the following ages, was to be under the influence of. 1. He observed the <hi type="italic">four winds to strive upon the great sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.2">v. 2</reference>. They strove which should blow strongest, and, at length, blow alone. This represents the contests among princes for empire, and the shakings of the nations by these contests, to which those mighty monarchies, which he was now to have a prospect of, owed their rise. One wind from any point of the compass, if it blow hard, will cause a great commotion in the sea; but what a tumult must needs be raised when the four winds strive for mastery! This is it which the kings of the nations are contending for in their wars, which are as noisy and violent as the battle of the winds; but how is the poor sea tossed and torn, how terrible are its concussions, and how violent its convulsions, while the winds are at strife which shall have the sole power of troubling it! Note, This world is like a stormy tempestuous sea; thanks to the proud ambitious winds that vex it. 2. He saw <hi type="italic">four great beasts come up from the sea,</hi> from the <hi type="italic">troubled waters,</hi> in which aspiring minds love to fish. The monarchs and monarchies are represented by <hi type="italic">beasts,</hi> because too often it is by brutish rage and tyranny that they are raised and supported. These beasts were <hi type="italic">diverse one from another</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.3">v. 3</reference>), of different shapes, to denote the different genius and complexion of the nations in whose hands they were lodged. (1.) <hi type="italic">The first</hi> beast <hi type="italic">was like a lion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.4">v. 4</reference>. This was the Chaldean monarchy, that was fierce and strong, and made the kings absolute. This lion had <hi type="italic">eagle's wings,</hi> with which to fly upon the prey, denoting the wonderful speed that Nebuchadnezzar made in his conquest of kingdoms. But Daniel soon sees the <hi type="italic">wings plucked,</hi> a full stop put to the career of their victorious arms. Divers countries that had been tributaries to them revolt from them, and make head against them; so that this monstrous animal, this winged lion, is made to <hi type="italic">stand upon the feet as a man, and a man's heart is given to it.</hi> It has lost the heart of a lion, which it had been famous for (one of our English kings was called <hi type="italic">Cœur de Lion—Lion-heart</hi>), has lost its courage and become feeble and faint, dreading every thing and daring nothing; they are put in fear, and made to know themselves to be but men. Sometimes the valour of a nation strangely sinks, and it becomes cowardly and effeminate, so that what was the head of the nations in an age or two becomes the tail. (2.) The <hi type="italic">second</hi> beast was <hi type="italic">like a bear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.5">v. 5</reference>. This was the Persian monarchy, less strong and generous than the former, but no less ravenous. This bear <hi type="italic">raised up itself on one side</hi> against the lion, and soon mastered it. It <hi type="italic">raised up one dominion;</hi> so some read it. Persia and Media, which in Nebuchadnezzar's image were the <hi type="italic">two arms</hi> in one breast, now set up a joint government. This bear had <hi type="italic">three ribs in the mouth of it between the teeth,</hi> the remains of those nations it had devoured, which were the marks of its voraciousness, and yet an indication that though it had devoured much it could not devour all; some ribs still stuck in the teeth of it, which it could not conquer. Whereupon it was said to it, "<hi type="italic">Arise, devour much flesh;</hi> let alone the bones, the ribs, that cannot be conquered, and set upon that which will be an easier prey." The princes will stir up both the kings and the people to push on their conquests, and let nothing stand before them. Note, Conquests, unjustly made, are but like those of the beasts of prey, and in <hi type="italic">this</hi> much worse, that the beasts prey not upon those of their own kind, as wicked and unreasonable men do. (3.) The third beast was <hi type="italic">like a leopard,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.6">v. 6</reference>. This was the Grecian monarchy, founded by <hi type="italic">Alexander the Great,</hi> active, crafty, and cruel, like a <hi type="italic">leopard.</hi> He had <hi type="italic">four wings of a fowl;</hi> the lion seems to have had but two wings; but the leopard had four, for though Nebuchadnezzar made great despatch in his conquests Alexander made much greater. In six years' time he gained the whole empire of Persia, a great part besides of Asia, made himself master of Syria, Egypt, India, and other nations. This beast had <hi type="italic">four heads;</hi> upon Alexander's death his conquests were divided among his four chief captains; Seleucus Nicanor had Asia the Great; Perdiccas, and after him Antigonus, had Asia the Less; Cassander had Macedonia; and Ptolemeus had Egypt. <hi type="italic">Dominion</hi> was <hi type="italic">given</hi> to this <hi type="italic">beast;</hi> it was given of God, from whom alone promotion comes. (4.) The fourth beast was more fierce, and formidable, and mischievous, than any of them, unlike any of the other, nor is there any among the beasts of prey to which it might be compared, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.7">v. 7</reference>. The learned are not agreed concerning this anonymous beast; some make it to be the Roman empire, which, when it was in its glory, comprehended ten kingdoms, Italy, France, Spain, Germany, Britain, Sarmatia, Pannonia, Asia, Greece, and Egypt; and then the little horn which rose by the fall of three of the other horns (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.8">v. 8</reference>) they make to be the Turkish empire, which rose in the room of Asia, Greece, and Egypt. Others make this fourth beast to be the kingdom of Syria, the family of the Seleucidæ, which was very cruel and oppressive to the people of the Jews, as we find in Josephus and the history of the Maccabees. And herein that empire was diverse from those which went before, that none of the preceding powers compelled the Jews to renounce their religion, but the kings of Syria did, and used them barbarously. Their armies and commanders were the <hi type="italic">great iron teeth</hi> with which they <hi type="italic">devoured and broke in pieces</hi> the people of God, and they <hi type="italic">trampled upon the residue</hi> of them. The <hi type="italic">ten horns</hi> are then supposed to be ten kings that reigned successively in Syria; and then the <hi type="italic">little horn</hi> is Antiochus Epiphanes, the last of the ten, who by one means or other undermined three of the kings, and got the government. He was a man of great ingenuity, and therefore is said to have eyes <hi type="italic">like the eyes of a man;</hi> and he was very bold and daring, had a <hi type="italic">mouth speaking great things.</hi> We shall meet with him again in these prophecies.
entries.c77eb799a354fcd199ee39e98a41b76a2de200f4: <div eID="gen19496" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Four Beasts. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 555.)</title> <div sID="gen19497" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> I beheld till the thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit, whose garment <hi type="italic">was</hi> white as snow, and the hair of his head like the pure wool: his throne <hi type="italic">was like</hi> the fiery flame, <hi type="italic">and</hi> his wheels <hi type="italic">as</hi> burning fire. <hi type="super">10</hi> A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him: thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened. <hi type="super">11</hi> I beheld then because of the voice of the great words which the horn spake: I beheld <hi type="italic">even</hi> till the beast was slain, and his body destroyed, and given to the burning flame. <hi type="super">12</hi> As concerning the rest of the beasts, they had their dominion taken away: yet their lives were prolonged for a season and time. <hi type="super">13</hi> I saw in the night visions, and, behold, <hi type="italic">one</hi> like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. <hi type="super">14</hi> And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him: his dominion <hi type="italic">is</hi> an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom <hi type="italic">that</hi> which shall not be destroyed. <div eID="gen19497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19498" type="x-p"/> Whether we understand the fourth beast to signify the Syrian empire, or the Roman, or the former as the figure of the latter, it is plain that these verses are intended for the comfort and support of the people of God in reference to the persecutions they were likely to sustain both from the one and from the other, and from all their proud enemies in every age; for it is written for their learning on whom the ends of the world have come, that they also, through patience and comfort of this scripture, might have hope. Three things are here discovered that are very encouraging:— <div eID="gen19498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19499" type="x-p"/> I. That there is a judgment to come, and God is the Judge. Now men have their day, and every pretender thinks he should have his day, and struggles for it. But <hi type="italic">he that sits in heaven laughs at them,</hi> for he sees that <hi type="italic">his day is coming,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.13">Ps. xxxvii. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">I beheld</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.9">v. 9</reference>) <hi type="italic">till the thrones were cast down,</hi> not only the thrones of these beasts, but <hi type="italic">all rule, authority, power,</hi> that are set up in opposition to the kingdom of God among men (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1 Cor. xv. 24</reference>): such are the thrones of the kingdoms of the world, in comparison with God's kingdom; those that see them set up need but wait awhile, and they will see them cast down. <hi type="italic">I beheld till thrones were set up</hi> (so it may as well be read), Christ's throne and the throne of his Father. One of the rabbin confesses that these thrones are <hi type="italic">set up,</hi> one for <hi type="italic">God,</hi> another for the <hi type="italic">Son of David.</hi> It is the <hi type="italic">judgment</hi> that is here <hi type="italic">set,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">v. 10</reference>. Now, 1. This is intended to proclaim God's wise and righteous government of the world by his providence; and an unspeakable satisfaction it gives to all good men, in the midst of the convulsions and revolutions of states and kingdoms, that <hi type="italic">the Lord has prepared his throne in the heavens and his kingdom rules over all</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.19">Ps. ciii. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">that verily there is a God that judges in the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.58.11">Ps. lviii. 11</reference>. 2. Perhaps it points at the destruction brought by the providence of God upon the empire of Syria, or that of Rome, for their tyrannizing over the people of God. But, 3. It seems principally designed to describe the last judgment, for though it follow not immediately upon the dominion of the fourth beast, nay, though it be yet to come, perhaps many ages to come, yet it was intended that in every age the people of God should encourage themselves, under their troubles, with the belief and prospect of it. Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of it, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.14">Jude 14</reference>. Does the mouth of the enemy <hi type="italic">speak great things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.8">v. 8</reference>. Here are far greater things which the mouth of the Lord has spoken. Many of the New-Testament predictions of the judgment to come have a plain allusion to this vision, especially St John's vision of it, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.11-Rev.20.12">Rev. xx. 11, 12</reference>. (1.) The Judge is <hi type="italic">the Ancient of days</hi> himself, <hi type="italic">God the Father,</hi> the glory of whose presence is here described. He is called <hi type="italic">the Ancient of days,</hi> because he is God <hi type="italic">from everlasting to everlasting.</hi> Among men we reckon that <hi type="italic">with the ancient is wisdom,</hi> and <hi type="italic">days shall speak;</hi> shall not all flesh then be silent before him who is <hi type="italic">the Ancient of days?</hi> The glory of the Judge is here set forth by his garment, which was <hi type="italic">white as snow,</hi> denoting his splendour and purity in all the administrations of his justice; and the <hi type="italic">hair of his head</hi> clean and white, <hi type="italic">as the pure wool,</hi> that, as the white and hoary head, he may appear venerable. (2.) The throne is very formidable. It is <hi type="italic">like the fiery flame,</hi> dreadful to the wicked that shall be summoned before it. And the throne being movable upon wheels, or at least the chariot in which he rode the circuit, the <hi type="italic">wheels</hi> thereof are <hi type="italic">as burning fire,</hi> to devour the adversaries; for <hi type="italic">our God is a consuming fire,</hi> and with him are <hi type="italic">everlasting burnings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">Isa. xxxiii. 14</reference>. This is enlarged upon, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">v. 10</reference>. As to all his faithful friends there <hi type="italic">proceeds out of the throne of God and the Lamb a pure river of water of life</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Rev. xxii. 1</reference>), so to all his implacable enemies there <hi type="italic">issues and comes forth from</hi> his throne a <hi type="italic">fiery stream, a stream of brimstone</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa. xxx. 33</reference>), a <hi type="italic">fire</hi> that shall <hi type="italic">devour before him.</hi> He is a swift witness, and his word a word upon the wheels. (3.) The attendants are numerous and very splendid. The Shechinah is always attended with angels; it is so here (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thousand thousands minister to him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">ten thousand times ten thousand stand before him.</hi> It is his glory that he has such attendants, but much more his glory that he neither needs them nor can be benefited by them. See how numerous the heavenly hosts are (there are <hi type="italic">thousands of angels</hi>), and how obsequious they are—they <hi type="italic">stand before God,</hi> ready to go on his errands and to take the first intimation of his will and pleasure. They will particularly be employed as ministers of his justice in the last judgment day, when the <hi type="italic">Son of man shall come, and all the holy angels with him.</hi> Enoch prophesied that the Lord should come <hi type="italic">with his holy myriads.</hi> (4.) The process is fair and unexceptionable: <hi type="italic">The judgment is set,</hi> publicly and openly, that all may have recourse to it; and <hi type="italic">the books are opened.</hi> As in courts of judgment among men the proceedings are in writing and upon record, which is laid open when the cause comes to a hearing, the examination of witnesses is produced, and affidavits are read, to clear the matter of fact, and the statute and common-law books are consulted to find out what is the law, so, in the judgment of the great day, the equity of the sentence will be as incontestably evident as if there were books opened to justify it. <div eID="gen19499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19500" type="x-p"/> II. That the proud and cruel enemies of the church of God will certainly be reckoned with and brought down in due time, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.11-Dan.7.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. This is here represented to us, 1. In the destroying of the fourth beast. God's quarrel with this beast is <hi type="italic">because of the voice of the great words which the horn spoke,</hi> bidding defiance to Heaven, and triumphing over all that is sacred; this provokes God more than any thing, for the <hi type="italic">enemy to behave himself proudly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.27">Deut. xxxii. 27</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> Pharaoh must be humbled, because he has said, <hi type="italic">Who is the Lord?</hi> and has said, <hi type="italic">I will pursue, I will overtake.</hi> Enoch foretold that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> the Lord would come to <hi type="italic">judge the world,</hi> that he might <hi type="italic">convince all that are ungodly of their hard speeches,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>. Note, Great words are but idle words, for which men must give account in the great day. And see what becomes of this beast that talks so big: He <hi type="italic">is slain,</hi> and <hi type="italic">his body destroyed and given to the burning flame.</hi> The Syrian empire, after Antiochus, was destroyed. He himself died of a miserable disease, his family was rooted out, the kingdom wasted by the Parthians and Armenians, and at length made a province of the Roman empire by Pompey. And the Roman empire itself (if we take that for the fourth beast), after it began to persecute Christianity, declined and wasted away, and the body of it was destroyed. <hi type="italic">So shall all thy enemies perish, O Lord!</hi> and be <hi type="italic">slain before thee.</hi> 2. In the diminishing and weakening of the other three beasts (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.12">v. 12</reference>): They had <hi type="italic">their dominion taken away,</hi> and so were disabled from doing the mischiefs they had done to the church and people of God; but <hi type="italic">a prolonging in life was given them, for a time and a season,</hi> a set time, the bounds of which they could not pass. The power of the foregoing kingdoms was quite broken, but the people of them still remained in a mean, weak, and low condition. We may allude to this in describing the remainders of sin in the hearts of good people; they have corruptions in them, the lives of which are prolonged, so that they are not perfectly free from sin, but the dominion of them is taken away, so that sin does not <hi type="italic">reign in their mortal bodies.</hi> And thus God deals with his church's enemies; sometimes he breaks the teeth of them (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.7">Ps. iii. 7</reference>), when he does not break the neck of them, crushes the persecution, but reprieves the persecutors, that they may have space to repent. And it is fit that God, in doing his own work, should take his own time and way. <div eID="gen19500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19501" type="x-p"/> III. That the kingdom of the Messiah shall be set up, and kept up, in the world, in spite of all the opposition of the powers of darkness. Let the heathen rage and fret as long as they please, God will <hi type="italic">set his King upon his holy hill of Zion.</hi> Daniel sees this in vision, and comforts himself and his friends with the prospect of it. This is the same with Nebuchadnezzar's foresight of the <hi type="italic">stone cut out of the mountain without hands,</hi> which broke in pieces the image; but in this vision there is much more of pure gospel than in that. 1. The Messiah is here called the Son of man—<hi type="italic">one like unto the Son of man;</hi> for he was <hi type="italic">made in the likeness of sinful flesh,</hi> was <hi type="italic">found in fashion as a man. I saw one like unto the Son of man,</hi> one exactly agreeing with the idea formed in the divine counsels of him that in the fulness of time was to be the Mediator between God and man. He is <hi type="italic">like unto the son of man,</hi> but is indeed the Son of God. Our Savior seems plainly to refer to this vision when he says (<reference osisRef="John.5.27">John v. 27</reference>) that the <hi type="italic">Father</hi> has therefore <hi type="italic">given him authority to execute judgment</hi> because he is <hi type="italic">the Son of man,</hi> and because he is the person whom Daniel saw in vision, to whom a kingdom and dominion were to be given. 2. He is said to <hi type="italic">come with the clouds of heaven.</hi> Some refer this to his incarnation; he descended <hi type="italic">in the clouds of heaven,</hi> came into the world unseen, as the glory of the Lord took possession of the temple in a cloud. The empires of the world were beasts that <hi type="italic">rose out of the sea;</hi> but Christ's kingdom is from above: he is the <hi type="italic">Lord from heaven.</hi> I think it is rather to be referred to his ascension; when he returned to the Father the eye of his disciples followed him, till <hi type="italic">a cloud received him out of their sight,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.1.9">Acts i. 9</reference>. He made that cloud his chariot, wherein he rode triumphantly to the upper world. He comes swiftly, irresistibly, and comes in state, for he <hi type="italic">comes with the clouds of heaven.</hi> 3. He is here represented as having a mighty interest in Heaven. When the cloud received him out of the sight of his disciples, it is worth while to enquire (as the sons of the prophets concerning Elijah in a like case) whither it carried him, where it lodged him; and here we are told, abundantly to our satisfaction, that <hi type="italic">he came to the Ancient of days;</hi> for he ascended to <hi type="italic">his Father and our Father,</hi> to <hi type="italic">his God and our God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.20.17">John xx. 17</reference>); from him he came forth, and to him he returns, to be glorified with him, and to sit down at his right hand. It was with a great deal of pleasure that he said, <hi type="italic">Now I go to him that sent me.</hi> But was he welcome? Yes, not doubt, he was, for <hi type="italic">they brought him near before him;</hi> he was introduced into his Father's presence, with the attendance and adorations of <hi type="italic">all the angels of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">Heb. i. 6</reference>. God <hi type="italic">caused him to draw near and approach to him,</hi> as an advocate and undertaker for us (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jer. xxx. 21</reference>), that we through him might be <hi type="italic">made nigh.</hi> By this solemn near approach which he made to the Ancient of days it appears that the Father accepted the sacrifice he offered, and the satisfaction he made, and was entirely well pleased with all he had done. He was <hi type="italic">brought near,</hi> as our high priest, who for us enters within the veil, and as our forerunner, 4. He is here represented as having a mighty influence upon this earth, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">v. 14</reference>. When he went to be glorified with his Father he had a <hi type="italic">power given him over all flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.2">John xvii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.5">5</reference>. With the prospect of this Daniel and his friends are here comforted, that not only the dominion of the church's enemies shall be taken away (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.12">v. 12</reference>), but the church's head and best friend shall have <hi type="italic">the dominion given him;</hi> to him <hi type="italic">every knee shall bow</hi> and <hi type="italic">every tongue confess.</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.9-Phil.2.10">Phil. ii. 9, 10</reference>. To him are given <hi type="italic">glory and a kingdom,</hi> and they are given by him who has an unquestionable right to give them, which, some think with an eye to these words, our Savior teaches us to acknowledge in the close of the Lord's prayer, <hi type="italic">For thine is the kingdom, the power, and the glory.</hi> It is here foretold that the kingdom of the exalted Redeemer shall be, (1.) A universal kingdom, the only universal monarchy, whatever others have pretended to, or aimed at: <hi type="italic">All people, nations, and languages,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">fear him,</hi> and be under his jurisdiction, either as his willing subjects or as his conquered captives, to be either ruled or overruled by him. One way or other, the kingdoms of the world shall all become his kingdoms. (2.) An everlasting kingdom. His <hi type="italic">dominion</hi> shall not <hi type="italic">pass away</hi> to any successor, much less to any invader, and his kingdom is <hi type="italic">that</hi> which <hi type="italic">shall not be destroyed.</hi> Even the gates of hell, or the infernal powers and policies, shall not prevail against it. The church shall continue militant to the end of time, and triumphant to the endless ages of eternity.
entries.4f0bb6efbd7327510f6b5837e0fe3524d1421383: <div eID="gen19501" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Four Beasts. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 555.)</title> <div sID="gen19502" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> I Daniel was grieved in my spirit in the midst of <hi type="italic">my</hi> body, and the visions of my head troubled me. <hi type="super">16</hi> I came near unto one of them that stood by, and asked him the truth of all this. So he told me, and made me know the interpretation of the things. <hi type="super">17</hi> These great beasts, which are four, <hi type="italic">are</hi> four kings, <hi type="italic">which</hi> shall arise out of the earth. <hi type="super">18</hi> But the saints of the most High shall take the kingdom, and possess the kingdom for ever, even for ever and ever. <hi type="super">19</hi> Then I would know the truth of the fourth beast, which was diverse from all the others, exceeding dreadful, whose teeth <hi type="italic">were of</hi> iron, and his nails <hi type="italic">of</hi> brass; <hi type="italic">which</hi> devoured, brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with his feet; <hi type="super">20</hi> And of the ten horns that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in his head, and <hi type="italic">of</hi> the other which came up, and before whom three fell; even <hi type="italic">of</hi> that horn that had eyes, and a mouth that spake very great things, whose look <hi type="italic">was</hi> more stout than his fellows. <hi type="super">21</hi> I beheld, and the same horn made war with the saints, and prevailed against them; <hi type="super">22</hi> Until the Ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the most High; and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom. <hi type="super">23</hi> Thus he said, The fourth beast shall be the fourth kingdom upon earth, which shall be diverse from all kingdoms, and shall devour the whole earth, and shall tread it down, and break it in pieces. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the ten horns out of this kingdom <hi type="italic">are</hi> ten kings <hi type="italic">that</hi> shall arise: and another shall rise after them; and he shall be diverse from the first, and he shall subdue three kings. <hi type="super">25</hi> And he shall speak <hi type="italic">great</hi> words against the most High, and shall wear out the saints of the most High, and think to change times and laws: and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and the dividing of time. <hi type="super">26</hi> But the judgment shall sit, and they shall take away his dominion, to consume and to destroy <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto the end. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the kingdom and dominion, and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven, shall be given to the people of the saints of the most High, whose kingdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him. <hi type="super">28</hi> Hitherto <hi type="italic">is</hi> the end of the matter. As for me Daniel, my cogitations much troubled me, and my countenance changed in me: but I kept the matter in my heart. <div eID="gen19502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19503" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. The deep impressions which these visions made upon the prophet. God in them put honour upon him, and gave him satisfaction, yet not without a great allay of pain and perplexity (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">I Daniel was grieved in my spirit, in the midst of my body.</hi> The word here used for the <hi type="italic">body</hi> properly signifies a <hi type="italic">sheath</hi> or <hi type="italic">scabbard,</hi> for the body is no more to the soul; that is the weapon; it is that which we are principally to take care of. The <hi type="italic">visions of my head troubled me,</hi> and again (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.28">v. 28</reference>), <hi type="italic">my cogitations much troubled me.</hi> The manner in which these things were discovered to him quite overwhelmed him, and put his thoughts so much to the stretch that his spirits failed him, and the trance he was in tired him and made him faint. The things themselves that were discovered amazed and astonished him, and put him into a confusion, till by degrees he recollected and conquered himself, and set the comforts of the vision over against the terrors of it. <div eID="gen19503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19504" type="x-p"/> II. His earnest desire to understand the meaning of them (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">I came near to one of those that stood by, to</hi> one of the angels that appeared attending the <hi type="italic">Son of man</hi> in his glory, and <hi type="italic">asked him the truth</hi> (the true intent and meaning) <hi type="italic">of all this.</hi> Note, It is a very desirable thing to take the right and full sense of what we see and hear from God; and those that would know must ask by faithful and fervent prayer and by <hi type="italic">accomplishing a diligent search.</hi> <div eID="gen19504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19505" type="x-p"/> III. The key that was given him, to let him into the understanding of this vision. The angel <hi type="italic">told him,</hi> and told him so plainly that he made him <hi type="italic">know the interpretation of the thing,</hi> and so made him somewhat more easy. <div eID="gen19505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19506" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">The great beasts</hi> are great <hi type="italic">kings</hi> and their kingdoms, great monarchs and their monarchies, <hi type="italic">which shall arise out of the earth,</hi> as those beasts did <hi type="italic">out of the sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.17">v. 17</reference>. They are but <hi type="italic">terræfilii—from beneath;</hi> they savour of the earth, and their foundation is <hi type="italic">in the dust;</hi> they are of the earth earthy, and they are written in the dust, and to the dust they shall return. <div eID="gen19506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19507" type="x-p"/> 2. Daniel pretty well understands the first three beasts, but concerning the fourth he desires to be better informed, because it differed so much from the rest, and was <hi type="italic">exceedingly dreadful,</hi> and not only so, but very mischievous, or it <hi type="italic">devoured and broke in pieces,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.19">v. 19</reference>. Perhaps it was this that put Daniel into such a fright, and this part of the visions of his head troubled him more than any of the rest. But especially he desired to know what the <hi type="italic">little horn</hi> was, that <hi type="italic">had eyes,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">mouth that spoke very great things,</hi> and whose countenance was more fearless and formidable than that of <hi type="italic">any of his fellows,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.20">v. 20</reference>. And this he was most inquisitive about because it was this horn that <hi type="italic">made war with the saints, and prevailed against them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.21">v. 21</reference>. While no more is intimated than that the children of men make war with one another, and prevail against one another, the prophet does not show himself so much concerned (<hi type="italic">let the potsherds strive with the potsherds of the earth,</hi> and be dashed in pieces one against another); but when they <hi type="italic">make war with the saints,</hi> when the <hi type="italic">precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold,</hi> are broken as <hi type="italic">earthen pitchers,</hi> it is time to ask, "What is the meaning of this? Will the Lord cast off his people? Will he suffer their enemies to trample upon them and triumph over them? What is this same horn that shall prevail so far against the saints?" To this his interpreter answers (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.23-Dan.7.25">v. 23-25</reference>) that this <hi type="italic">fourth beast</hi> is a <hi type="italic">fourth kingdom,</hi> that <hi type="italic">shall devour the whole earth,</hi> or (as it may be read) <hi type="italic">the whole land.</hi> That the <hi type="italic">ten horns are ten kings,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">little horn</hi> is another king that shall subdue three kings, and shall be very abusive to God and his people, shall act, (1.) Very impiously towards God. He shall <hi type="italic">speak great words against the Most High,</hi> setting him, and his authority and justice, at defiance. (2.) Very imperiously towards the people of God. He shall <hi type="italic">wear out the saints of the Most High;</hi> he will not cut them off at once, but wear them out by long oppressions and a constant course of hardships put upon them, ruining their estates and weakening their families. The design of Satan has been to <hi type="italic">wear out the saints of the Most High,</hi> that they may be no more in remembrance; but the attempt is vain, for while the world stands God will have a church in it. He shall <hi type="italic">think to change times and laws,</hi> to abolish all the ordinances and institutions of religion, and to bring every body to say and do just as he would have them. He shall trample upon laws and customs, human and divine. <hi type="italic">Diruit, ædificut, mutat quadrata rotundis—He pulls down, he builds, he changes square into round,</hi> as if he meant to alter even the ordinances of heaven themselves. And in these daring attempts he shall for a time prosper and have success; they shall be given into his hand <hi type="italic">until time, times, and half a time</hi> (that is, for three years and a half), that famous prophetical measure of time which we meet with in the Revelation, which is sometimes called forty-two months, sometimes 1260 days, which come all to one. But at the end of that time the <hi type="italic">judgment shall sit and take away his dominion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.26">v. 26</reference>), which he expounds (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.11">v. 11</reference>) of the beast being <hi type="italic">slain and his body destroyed.</hi> And (as Mr. Mede reads <reference osisRef="Dan.7.12">v. 12</reference>) <hi type="italic">as to the rest of the beast,</hi> the ten horns, especially the little <hi type="italic">ruffling</hi> horn (as he calls it), they had their dominion taken away. Now the question is, Who is this enemy, whose rise, reign, and ruin, are foretold? Interpreters are not agreed. Some will have the fourth kingdom to be that of the Seleucidæ, and the little horn to be Antiochus, and show the accomplishment of all this in the history of the Maccabees; so Junius, Piscator, Polanus, Broughton, and many others: but others will have the fourth kingdom to be that of the Romans, and the <hi type="italic">little horn</hi> to be Julius Cæsar, and the succeeding emperors (says Calvin), the antichrist, the papal kingdom (says Mr. Joseph Mede), that <hi type="italic">wicked one,</hi> which, as this <hi type="italic">little horn,</hi> is to be consumed by the <hi type="italic">brightness of Christ's second coming.</hi> The pope assumes a power to <hi type="italic">change times and laws, potestas</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">autokratorike</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">an absolute and despotic power,</hi> as he calls it. Others make the <hi type="italic">little horn</hi> to be the <hi type="italic">Turkish empire;</hi> so Luther, Vatablus, and others. Now I cannot prove either side to be wrong; and therefore, since prophecies sometimes have many fulfillings, and we ought to give scripture its full latitude (in this as in many other controversies), I am willing to allow that they are both in the right, and that this prophecy has primary reference to the Syrian empire, and was intended for the encouragement of the Jews who suffered under Antiochus, that they might see even these melancholy times foretold, but might foresee a glorious issue of them at last, and the final overthrow of their proud oppressors; and, which is best of all, might foresee, not long after, the setting up of the kingdom of the Messiah in the world, with the hopes of which it was usual with the former prophets to comfort the people of God in their distresses. But yet it has a further reference, and foretels the like persecuting power and rage in Rome heathen, and no less in Rome papal, against the Christian religion, that was in Antiochus against the pious Jews and their religion. And St. John, in his visions and prophecies, which point primarily at Rome, has plain reference, in many particulars, to these visions of Daniel. <div eID="gen19507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19508" type="x-p"/> 3. He has a joyful prospect given him of the prevalency of God's kingdom among men, and its victory over all opposition at last. And it is very observable that in the midst of the predictions of the force and fury of the enemies this is brought in abruptly (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.18">v. 18</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.7.22">again v. 22</reference>), before it comes, in the course of the vision, to be interpreted, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.26-Dan.7.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. And this also refers, (1.) To the prosperous days of the Jewish church, after it had weathered the storm under Antiochus, and the power which the Maccabees obtained over their enemies. (2.) To the setting up of the kingdom of the Messiah in the world by the preaching of his gospel. <hi type="italic">For judgment Christ comes into this world,</hi> to rule by his Spirit, and to make all his saints <hi type="italic">kings and priests to their God.</hi> (3.) To the second coming of Jesus Christ, when the saints shall judge the world, shall sit down with him on his throne and triumph in the complete downfall of the devil's kingdom. Let us see what is here foretold. [1.] <hi type="italic">The Ancient of days shall come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.22">v. 22</reference>. God shall judge the world by his Son, to whom he has <hi type="italic">committed all judgment,</hi> and, as an earnest of that, he <hi type="italic">comes</hi> for the deliverance of his oppressed people, comes for the setting up of his kingdom in the world. [2.] <hi type="italic">The judgment shall sit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.26">v. 26</reference>. God will make it appear that he <hi type="italic">judges in the earth,</hi> and will, both in wisdom and in equity, plead his people's righteous cause. At the great day he will <hi type="italic">judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he has ordained.</hi> [3.] The <hi type="italic">dominion</hi> of the enemy shall be <hi type="italic">taken away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.26">v. 26</reference>. All Christ's enemies shall be made his footstool, and shall be <hi type="italic">consumed and destroyed</hi> to the end: these were the apostle uses concerning the man of sin, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2 Thess. ii. 8</reference>. He shall be <hi type="italic">consumed</hi> with the <hi type="italic">spirit of Christ's mouth</hi> and <hi type="italic">destroyed with the brightness of his coming.</hi> [4.] <hi type="italic">Judgment is given to the saints of the Most High.</hi> The apostles are entrusted with the preaching of a gospel by which the <hi type="italic">world shall be judged.</hi> All the saints by their faith and obedience condemn an unbelieving disobedient world; in Christ their head they shall judge the world, shall <hi type="italic">judge the twelve tribes of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Matt. xix. 28</reference>. See what reason we have to honour those that fear the Lord; how mean and despicable soever the saints now appear in the eye of the world, and how much contempt soever is poured upon them; they are the <hi type="italic">saints of the Most High;</hi> they are near and dear to God, and he owns them for his, and <hi type="italic">judgment</hi> is <hi type="italic">given to them.</hi> [5.] That which is most insisted upon is that <hi type="italic">the saints of the Most High shall take the kingdom, and possess the kingdom for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.18">v. 18</reference>. And again (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.22">v. 22</reference>), The <hi type="italic">time came that the saints possessed the kingdom.</hi> And again (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.27">v. 27</reference>), The <hi type="italic">kingdom and dominion, and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heavens, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High.</hi> Far be it from us to infer hence that dominion is founded on grace, or that this will warrant any, under pretence of saintship, to usurp kingship. No; <hi type="italic">Christ's kingdom is not of this world;</hi> but this intimates the spiritual dominion of the saints over their own lusts and corruptions, their victories over Satan and his temptations, and the triumphs of the martyrs over death and its terrors. It likewise promises that the gospel kingdom shall be set up, a kingdom of grace, the privileges and comforts of which now, <hi type="italic">under the heavens,</hi> shall be the earnest and first-fruits of the kingdom of <hi type="italic">glory in the heavens.</hi> When the empire became Christian, and princes used their power for the defence and advancement of Christianity, then the <hi type="italic">saints possessed the kingdom.</hi> The saints rule by the Spirit's ruling in them (and <hi type="italic">this is the victory overcoming the world, even their faith</hi>) and by making the kingdoms of this world to become Christ's kingdom. But the full accomplishment of this will be in the everlasting happiness of the saints, the kingdom that cannot be moved, which we, according to his promise, look for (that is the <hi type="italic">greatness of the kingdom</hi>), the crown of glory that fades not away—that is the <hi type="italic">everlasting kingdom.</hi> See what an emphasis is laid upon this (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.18">v. 18</reference>): The saints shall possess the kingdom <hi type="italic">for ever, even for ever and ever;</hi> and the reason is because he whose saints they are is the <hi type="italic">Most High</hi> and <hi type="italic">his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.27">v. 27</reference>. He is so, and therefore theirs shall be so. <hi type="italic">Because I live, you shall live also,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.19">John xiv. 19</reference>. His kingdom is theirs; they reckon themselves exalted in his exaltation, and desire no greater honour and satisfaction to themselves than that <hi type="italic">all dominions</hi> should <hi type="italic">serve and obey him,</hi> as they shall do, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.27">v. 27</reference>. They shall either be brought into subjection to his golden sceptre or brought to destruction by his iron rod. <div eID="gen19508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19509" type="x-p"/> Daniel, in the close, when he ends that matter, tells us what impressions this vision made upon him; it overwhelmed his spirits to such a degree that his <hi type="italic">countenance</hi> was <hi type="italic">changed,</hi> and it made him look pale; but he <hi type="italic">kept the matter in his heart.</hi> Note, The heart must be the treasury and store-house of divine things; there we must hide God's word, as the Virgin Mary kept the sayings of Christ, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.51">Luke ii. 51</reference>. Daniel kept <hi type="italic">the matter in his heart,</hi> with a design, not to keep it from the church, but to keep it for the church, that what he had received from the Lord he might fully and faithfully deliver to the people. Note, It concerns God's prophets and ministers to treasure up the things of God in their minds, and there to digest them well. If we would have God's word ready in our mouths when we have occasion for it, we must keep it in our hearts at all times.  <chapter eID="Dan.7"/> <div eID="gen19509" type="x-p"/>

entries.1a61d7d02ee591155cf9a91fc03d9db5ffc46b87: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12088"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Dan.7.1-Dan.7.28">Da 7:1-28</reference>. Vision of the Four Beasts.</title> <div sID="gen21861" type="x-p"/> This chapter treats of the same subject as the second chapter. But there the four kingdoms, and Messiah's final kingdom, were regarded according to their external political aspect, but here according to the mind of God concerning them, and their moral features. The outward political history had been shown in its general features to the world ruler, whose position fitted him for receiving such a revelation. But God's prophet here receives disclosures as to the characters of the powers of the world, in a religious point of view, suited to his position and receptivity. Hence in the second chapter the images are taken from the inanimate sphere; in the seventh chapter they are taken from the animate. Nebuchadnezzar saw superficially the world power as a splendid human figure, and the kingdom of God as a mere stone at the first. Daniel sees the world kingdoms in their inner essence as of an animal nature lower than human, being estranged from God; and that only in the kingdom of God ("the Son of man," the representative man) is the true dignity of man realized. So, as contrasted with Nebuchadnezzar's vision, the kingdom of God appears to Daniel, from the very first, superior to the world kingdom. For though in physical force the beasts excel man, man has essentially spiritual powers. Nebuchadnezzar's colossal image represents mankind in its own strength, but only the outward man. Daniel sees man spiritually degraded to the beast level, led by blind impulses, through his alienation from God. It is only from above that the perfect Son of man comes, and in His kingdom man attains his true destiny. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9">Psa 8:1-9</reference> with <reference osisRef="Gen.1.26-Gen.1.28">Ge 1:26-28</reference>. Humanity is impossible without divinity: it sinks to bestiality (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.9">Psa 32:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.20">49:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.22">73:22</reference>). Obstinate heathen nations are compared to "bulls" (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.30">Psa 68:30</reference>); Egypt to the dragon in the Nile (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Is 27:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">51:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Eze 29:3</reference>). The animal with all its sagacity looks always to the ground, without consciousness of relation to God. What elevates man is communion with God, in willing subjection to Him. The moment he tries to exalt himself to independence of God, as did Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.30">Da 4:30</reference>), he sinks to the beast's level. Daniel's acquaintance with the animal colossal figures in Babylon and Nineveh was a psychological preparation for his animal visions. <reference osisRef="Hos.13.7">Ho 13:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.8">8</reference> would occur to him while viewing those ensigns of the world power. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.2.15">Jr 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.6">5:6</reference>.<div eID="gen21861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21862" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12088"/><hi type="bold">1. Belshazzar--</hi>Good Hebrew manuscripts have "Belshazzar"; meaning "Bel is to be burnt with hostile fire" (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.2">Jr 50:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.44">51:44</reference>). In the history he is called by his ordinary name; in the prophecy, which gives his true destiny, he is called a corresponding name, by the change of a letter.<div eID="gen21862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21863" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">visions of his head--</hi>not confused "dreams," but distinct images seen while his mind was collected.<div eID="gen21863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sum--</hi>a "summary." In predictions, generally, details are not given so fully as to leave no scope for free agency, faith, and patient waiting for God manifesting His will in the event. He "wrote" it for the Church in all ages; he "told" it for the comfort of his captive fellow countrymen. <div eID="gen21864" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fea0588a551627175ad9920b890c1d5f025a52a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12089"/><div sID="gen21865" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12089"/><hi type="bold">2. the four winds--</hi>answering to the "four beasts"; their several conflicts in the four quarters or directions of the world.<div eID="gen21865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strove--</hi>burst forth (from the abyss) [Maurer].<div eID="gen21866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21867" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sea--</hi>The world powers rise out of the agitations of the political sea (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.7">Jr 46:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.21.25">Lu 21:25</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.13.1">Re 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.15">17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">21:1</reference>); the kingdom of God and the Son of man from the clouds of heaven (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Da 7:13</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="John.8.23">Joh 8:23</reference>). Tregelles takes "the great sea" to mean, as always elsewhere in Scripture (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.4">Jos 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.1">9:1</reference>), the Mediterranean, the center territorially of the four kingdoms of the vision, which all border on it and have Jerusalem subject to them. Babylon did not border on the Mediterranean, nor rule Jerusalem, till Nebuchadnezzar's time, when both things took place simultaneously. Persia encircled more of this sea, namely, from the Hellespont to Cyrene. Greece did not become a monarchy before Alexander's time, but then, succeeding to Persia, it became mistress of Jerusalem. It surrounded still more of the Mediterranean, adding the coasts of Greece to the part held by Persia. Rome, under Augustus, realized three things at once--it became a monarchy; it became mistress of the last of the four parts of Alexander's empire (symbolized by the four heads of the third beast), and of Jerusalem; it surrounded all the Mediterranean. <div eID="gen21867" type="x-p"/>
entries.24a69c4e63ea26d395be9886fba9b83cbf6471cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12090"/><div sID="gen21868" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12090"/><hi type="bold">3. beasts--</hi>not living animals, as the cherubic four in <reference osisRef="Rev.4.7">Re 4:7</reference> (for the original is a different word from "beasts," and ought to be there translated, living animals). The cherubic living animals represent redeemed man, combining in himself the highest forms of animal life. But the "beasts" here represent the world powers, in their beast-like, grovelling character. It is on the fundamental harmony between nature and spirit, between the three kingdoms of nature, history, and revelation, that Scripture symbolism rests. The selection of symbols is not arbitrary, but based on the essence of things. <div eID="gen21868" type="x-p"/>
entries.98a36549900670e00c60a33d8b1901a83cddd1b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12091"/><div sID="gen21869" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12091"/><hi type="bold">4. lion--</hi>the symbol of strength and courage; chief among the kingdoms, as the lion among the beasts. Nebuchadnezzar is called "the lion" (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.7">Jr 4:7</reference>).<div eID="gen21869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21870" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eagle's wings--</hi>denoting a widespread and rapidly acquired (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.11">Is 46:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.13">Jr 4:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.19">La 4:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.6">Ha 1:6</reference>) empire (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jr 48:40</reference>).<div eID="gen21870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21871" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plucked--</hi>Its ability for widespread conquests passed away under Evil-merodach, &c. [Grotius]; rather, during Nebuchadnezzar's privation of his throne, while deranged.<div eID="gen21871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21872" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it was lifted up from the earth--</hi>that is, from its grovelling bestiality.<div eID="gen21872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21873" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made stand ... as a man--</hi>So long as Nebuchadnezzar, in haughty pride, relied on his own strength, he forfeited the true dignity of man, and was therefore degraded to be with the beasts. <reference osisRef="Dan.4.16">Da 4:16</reference>: "Let his heart be changed from man's, and let a beast's heart be given unto him." But after he learned by this sore discipline that "the Most High ruleth in the kingdom of men" (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.35">Da 4:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.36">36</reference>), the change took place in him, "a man's heart is given to him; instead of his former beast's heart, he attains man's true position, namely, to be consciously dependent on God." Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.9.20">Psa 9:20</reference>. <div eID="gen21873" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae1e394dd877737ae51b7e47742320cce4861035: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12092"/><div sID="gen21874" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12092"/><hi type="bold">5. bear--</hi>symbolizing the austere life of the Persians in their mountains, also their cruelty (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.17">Is 13:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.18">18</reference>; Cambyses, Ochus, and other of the Persian princes were notoriously cruel; the Persian laws involved, for one man's offense, the whole kindred and neighborhood in destruction, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.24">Da 6:24</reference>) and rapacity. "A bear is an all-devouring animal" [Aristotle, 8.5], (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.48">Jr 51:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.56">56</reference>).<div eID="gen21874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21875" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">raised ... itself on one side--</hi>but the Hebrew, "It raised up one dominion." The Medes, an ancient people, and the Persians, a modern tribe, formed one united sovereignty in contrast to the third and fourth kingdoms, each originally one, afterwards divided. English Version is the result of a slight change of a Hebrew letter. The idea then would be, "It lay on one of its fore feet, and stood on the other"; a figure still to be seen on one of the stones of Babylon [Munter, The Religion of Babylonia, 112]; denoting a kingdom that had been at rest, but is now rousing itself for conquest. Media is the lower side, passiveness; Persia, the upper, active element [Auberlen]. The three ribs in its mouth are Media, Lydia, and Babylon, brought under the Persian sway. Rather, Babylon, Lydia, and Egypt, not properly parts of its body, but seized by Medo-Persia [Sir Isaac Newton]. Called "ribs" because they strengthened the Medo-Persian empire. "Between its teeth," as being much grinded by it.<div eID="gen21875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21876" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">devour much flesh--</hi>that is, subjugate many nations. <div eID="gen21876" type="x-p"/>
entries.71142232bcb61d8d914f2e23b382e49ca5bb9a11: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12093"/><div sID="gen21877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12093"/><hi type="bold">6. leopard--</hi>smaller than the lion; swift (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.8">Ha 1:8</reference>); cruel (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.6">Is 11:6</reference>), the opposite of tame; springing suddenly from its hiding place on its prey (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.7">Ho 13:7</reference>); spotted. So Alexander, a small king, of a small kingdom, Macedon, attacked Darius at the head of the vast empire reaching from the Ægean Sea to the Indies. In twelve years he subjugated part of Europe, and all Asia from Illyricum and the Adriatic to the Ganges, not so much fighting as conquering [Jerome]. Hence, whereas Babylon is represented with two wings, Macedon has four, so rapid were its conquests. The various spots denote the various nations incorporated into his empire [Bochart]; or Alexander's own variation in character, at one time mild, at another cruel, now temperate, and now drunken and licentious.<div eID="gen21877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">four heads--</hi>explained in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.8">Da 8:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.22">22</reference>; the four kingdoms of the Diadochi or "successors" into which the Macedonian empire was divided at the death of Alexander, namely, Macedon and Greece under Cassander, Thrace and Bithynia under Lysimachus, Egypt under Ptolemy, and Syria under Seleucus.<div eID="gen21878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dominion ... given to it--</hi>by God; not by Alexander's own might. For how unlikely it was that thirty thousand men should overthrow several hundreds of thousands! Josephus [Antiquities, 11.6] says that Alexander adored the high priest of Jerusalem, saying that he at Dium in Macedonia had seen a vision of God so habited, inviting him to go to Asia, and promising him success. <div eID="gen21879" type="x-p"/>
entries.25602a4b8f2bbe085f99d5d2ec7461e0b85b3b8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12094"/><div sID="gen21880" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12094"/><hi type="bold">7. As Daniel lived under the kingdom of the first beast, and therefore needed not to describe it, and as the second and third are described fully in the second part of the book, the chief emphasis falls on the fourth. Also prophecy most dwells on the end, which is the consummation of the preceding series of events. It is in the fourth that the world power manifests fully its God-opposing nature. Whereas the three former kingdoms were designated respectively, as a lion, bear, and leopard, no particular beast is specified as the image of the fourth; for Rome is so terrible as to be not describable by any one, but combines in itself all that we can imagine inexpressibly fierce in all beasts. Hence thrice (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.7">Da 7:7</reference>, 19, 23) it is repeated, that the fourth was "diverse from all" the others. The formula of introduction, "I saw in the night visions," occurs here, as at <reference osisRef="Dan.7.2">Da 7:2</reference>, and again at <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Da 7:13</reference>, thus dividing the whole vision into three parts--</hi>the first embracing the three kingdoms, the second the fourth and its overthrow, the third Messiah's kingdom. The first three together take up a few centuries; the fourth, thousands of years. The whole lower half of the image in the second chapter is given to it. And whereas the other kingdoms consist of only one material, this consists of two, iron and clay (on which much stress is laid, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.41-Dan.2.43">Da 2:41-43</reference>); the "iron teeth" here allude to one material in the fourth kingdom of the image.<div eID="gen21880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21881" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ten horns--</hi>It is with the crisis, rather than the course, of the fourth kingdom that this seventh chapter is mainly concerned. The ten kings (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.24">Da 7:24</reference>, the "horns" representing power), that is, kingdoms, into which Rome was divided on its incorporation with the Germanic and Slavonic tribes, and again at the Reformation, are thought by many to be here intended. But the variation of the list of the ten, and their ignoring the eastern half of the empire altogether, and the existence of the Papacy before the breaking up of even the Western empire, instead of being the "little horn" springing up after the other ten, are against this view. The Western Roman empire continued till A.D. 731, and the Eastern, till A.D. 1453. The ten kingdoms, therefore, prefigured by the ten "toes" (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.41">Da 2:41</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.13.1">Re 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.12">17:12</reference>), are the ten kingdoms into which Rome shall be found finally divided when Antichrist shall appear [Tregelles]. These, probably, are prefigured by the number ten being the prevalent one at the chief turning points of Roman history. <div eID="gen21881" type="x-p"/>
entries.cd04283bceeb4509898f9d58b25cd42d0bf82ce8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12095"/><div sID="gen21882" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12095"/><hi type="bold">8. little horn--</hi>little at first, but afterwards waxing greater than all others. He must be sought "among them," namely, the ten horns. The Roman empire did not represent itself as a continuation of Alexander's; but the Germanic empire calls itself "the holy Roman empire." Napoleon's attempted universal monarchy was avowedly Roman: his son was called king of Rome. The czar (Cæsar) also professes to represent the eastern half of the Roman empire. The Roman civilization, church, language, and law are the chief elements in Germanic civilization. But the Romanic element seeks universal empire, while the Germanic seeks individualization. Hence the universal monarchies attempted by the Papacy, Charlemagne, Charles V, and Napoleon have failed, the iron not amalgamating with the clay. In the king symbolized by "the little horn," the God-opposing, haughty spirit of the world, represented by the fourth monarchy, finds its intensest development. "The man of sin," "the son of perdition" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3">2Th 2:3</reference>). Antichrist (<reference osisRef="1John.2.18">1Jo 2:18</reference>, 22; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.3">4:3</reference>). It is the complete evolution of the evil principle introduced by the fall.<div eID="gen21882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21883" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">three of the first horns plucked up--</hi>the exarchate of Ravenna, the kingdom of the Lombards and the state of Rome, which constituted the Pope's dominions at the first; obtained by Pope Zachary and Stephen II in return for acknowledging the usurper Pepin lawful king of France [Newton]. See Tregelles' objections, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.7">Da 7:7</reference>, "ten horns," Note. The "little horn," in his view, is to be Antichrist rising three and a half years before Christ's second advent, having first overthrown three of the ten contemporaneous kingdoms, into which the fourth monarchy, under which we live, shall be finally divided. Popery seems to be a fulfilment of the prophecy in many particulars, the Pope claiming to be God on earth and above all earthly dominions; but the spirit of Antichrist prefigured by Popery will probably culminate in ONE individual, to be destroyed by Christ's coming; He will be the product of the political world powers, whereas Popery which prepares His way, is a Church become worldly.<div eID="gen21883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21884" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eyes of man--</hi>Eyes express intelligence (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.18">Eze 1:18</reference>); so (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.5">Ge 3:5</reference>) the serpent's promise was, man's "eyes should be opened," if he would but rebel against God. Antichrist shall consummate the self-apotheosis, begun at the fall, high intellectual culture, independent of God. The metals representing Babylon and Medo-Persia, gold and silver, are more precious than brass and iron, representing Greece and Rome; but the latter metals are more useful to civilization (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.22">Ge 4:22</reference>). The clay, representing the Germanic element, is the most plastic material. Thus there is a progress in culture; but this is not a progress necessarily in man's truest dignity, namely, union and likeness to God. Nay, it has led him farther from God, to self-reliance and world-love. The beginnings of civilization were among the children of Cain (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.17-Gen.4.24">Ge 4:17-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.16.8">Lu 16:8</reference>). Antiochus Epiphanes, the first Antichrist, came from civilized Greece, and loved art. As Hellenic civilization produced the first, so modern civilization under the fourth monarchy will produce the last Antichrist. The "mouth" and "eyes" are those of a man, while the symbol is otherwise brutish, that is, it will assume man's true dignity, namely, wear the guise of the kingdom of God (which comes as the "Son of man" from above), while it is really bestial, namely, severed from God. Antichrist promises the same things as Christ, but in an opposite way: a caricature of Christ, offering a regenerated world without the cross. Babylon and Persia in their religion had more reverence for things divine than Greece and Rome in the imperial stages of their history. Nebuchadnezzar's human heart, given him (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.16">Da 4:16</reference>) on his repentance, contrasts with the human eyes of Antichrist, the pseudo son of man, namely, intellectual culture, while heart and mouth blaspheme God. The deterioration politically corresponds: the first kingdom, an organic unity; the second, divided into Median and Persian; the third branches off into four; the fourth, into ten. The two eastern kingdoms are marked by nobler metals; the two western, by baser; individualization and division appear in the latter, and it is they which produce the two Antichrists. <div eID="gen21884" type="x-p"/>
entries.8306c344aef2a2d687dcd3e512aca9632eb3cd6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12096"/><div sID="gen21885" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12096"/><hi type="bold">9. I beheld till--</hi>I continued looking till.<div eID="gen21885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thrones ... cast down--</hi>rather, "thrones were placed" [Vulgate and Luther], namely, for the saints and elect angels to whom "judgment is given" (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.22">Da 7:22</reference>), as assessors with the Judge. Compare <reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">Da 7:10</reference>, "thousand thousands ministered unto Him" (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mt 19:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.30">Lu 22:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2">1Co 6:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.21">1Ti 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.26">Re 2:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">4:4</reference>). In English Version the thrones cast down are those of the previously mentioned kings who give place to Messiah.<div eID="gen21886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21887" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ancient of days--</hi>"The everlasting Father" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>). He is the Judge here, as THE Son does not judge in His own cause, and it is His cause which is the one at issue with Antichrist.<div eID="gen21887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sit--</hi>the attitude of a judge about to pass sentence.<div eID="gen21888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21889" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">white--</hi>The judicial purity of the Judge, and of all things round Him, is hereby expressed (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.14">Re 1:14</reference>).<div eID="gen21889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wheels--</hi>as Oriental thrones move on wheels. Like the rapid flame, God's judgments are most swift in falling where He wills them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.15">Eze 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>). The judgment here is not the last judgment, for then there will be no beast, and heaven and earth shall have passed away; but it is that on Antichrist (the last development of the fourth kingdom), typical of the last judgment: Christ coming to substitute the millennial kingdom of glory for that of the cross (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.12-Rev.14.19">Re 17:12-14; 19</reference>:15-21; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">11:15</reference>). <div eID="gen21890" type="x-p"/>
entries.d7c6b24444949bbf167741454f46e97f2c1e2ddf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12097"/><div sID="gen21891" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12097"/><hi type="bold">10. thousand ... ministered unto him--</hi>so at the giving of the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">De 33:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Psa 68:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">He 12:22</reference>; Jude 14).<div eID="gen21891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ten ... thousand before him--</hi>image from the Sanhedrim, in which the father of the consistory sat with his assessors on each side, in the form of a semicircle, and the people standing before him.<div eID="gen21892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment was set--</hi>The judges sat (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.4">Re 20:4</reference>).<div eID="gen21893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">books ... opened--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.20.12">Re 20:12</reference>). Forensic image; all the documents of the cause at issue, connected with the condemnation of Antichrist and his kingdom, and the setting up of Messiah's kingdom. Judgment must pass on the world as being under the curse, before the glory comes; but Antichrist offers glory without the cross, a renewed world without the world being judged. <div eID="gen21894" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b8435a77c322e02385e13fe106fe70b6e949f75: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12098"/><div sID="gen21895" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12098"/>11. Here is set forth the execution on earth of the judgment pronounced in the unseen heavenly court of judicature (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.9">Da 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen21895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">body ... given to ... flame--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.19.20">Re 19:20</reference>). <div eID="gen21896" type="x-p"/>
entries.06946e0d778e72ce1e84edb7ddb778448e1a748e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12099"/><div sID="gen21897" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12099"/><hi type="bold">12. the rest of the beasts--</hi>that is, the three first, had passed away not by direct destroying judgments, such as consumed the little horn, as being the finally matured evil of the fourth beast. They had continued to exist but their "dominion was was taken away"; whereas the fourth beast shall cease utterly, superseded by Messiah's kingdom.<div eID="gen21897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for a season ... time--</hi>Not only the triumph of the beasts over the godly, but their very existence is limited to a definite time, and that time the exactly suitable one (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.24.22">Mt 24:22</reference>). Probably a definite period is meant by a "season and time" (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Da 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.3">Re 20:3</reference>). It is striking, the fourth monarchy, though Christianized for fifteen hundred years past, is not distinguished from the previous heathen monarchies, or from its own heathen portion. Nay, it is represented as the most God-opposed of all, and culminating at last in blasphemous Antichrist. The reason is: Christ's kingdom now is not of this world (<reference osisRef="John.18.36">Joh 18:36</reference>); and only at the second advent of Christ does it become an external power of the world. Hence Daniel, whose province it was to prophesy of the world powers, does not treat of Christianity until it becomes a world power, namely, at the second advent.
