The kingdom of God is a hidden one till Jesus comes again (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.17">Ro 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.2">Col 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.3.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.11">2Ti 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>). Rome was worldly while heathen, and remains worldly, though Christianized. So the New Testament views the present æon or age of the world as essentially heathenish, which we cannot love without forsaking Christ (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.2">Ro 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">1Co 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.8">2:6, 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">3:18</reference>; 7:31; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Co 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.4">Ga 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10">2Ti 4:10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1John.2.15">1Jo 2:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">17</reference>). The object of Christianity is not so much to Christianize the present world as to save souls out of it, so as not to be condemned with the world (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.32">1Co 11:32</reference>), but to rule with Him in His millennium (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.5">Mt 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.32">Lu 12:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.28-Luke.22.30">22:28-30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.17">Ro 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2">1Co 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Re 1:6</reference>; 2:26-28; 3:21; 20:4). This is to be our hope, not to reign in the present world course (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.8">1Co 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.18">2Co 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.14">He 13:14</reference>). There must be a "regeneration" of the world, as of the individual, a death previous to a resurrection, a destruction of the world kingdoms, before they rise anew as the kingdoms of Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mt 19:28</reference>). Even the millennium will not perfectly eradicate the world's corruption; another apostasy and judgment will follow (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.7-Rev.20.15">Re 20:7-15</reference>), in which the world of nature is to be destroyed and renewed, as the world of history was before the millennium (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.8-2Pet.3.13">2Pe 3:8-13</reference>); then comes the perfect earth and heaven (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">Re 21:1</reference>). Thus there is an onward progress, and the Christian is waiting for the consummation (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.33-Mark.13.37">Mr 13:33-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.35">Lu 12:35</reference>, 36, 40-46; <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.9">1Th 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>), as His Lord also is "expecting" (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.13">He 10:13</reference>). <div eID="gen21898" type="x-p"/>
entries.d84b7ca1e854c69e050e3ffb0046c705c9e878ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12100"/><div sID="gen21899" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12100"/><hi type="bold">13. Son of man--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.2.1">Eze 2:1</reference>). Not merely Son of David, and King of Israel, but Head of restored humanity (corresponding to the world-wide horizon of Daniel's prophecy); the seed of the woman, crushing Antichrist, the seed of the serpent, according to the Prot-evangel in Paradise (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Ge 3:15</reference>). The Representative Man shall then realize the original destiny of man as Head of the creation (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.26">Ge 1:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">28</reference>); the center of unity to Israel and the Gentiles. The beast, which taken conjointly represents the four beasts, ascends from the sea (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.2">Da 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.1">Re 13:1</reference>); the Son of man descends from "heaven." Satan, as the serpent, is the representative head of all that bestial; man, by following the serpent, has become bestial. God must, therefore, become man, so that man may cease to be beast-like. Whoever rejects the incarnate God will be judged by the Son of man just because He is the Son of man (<reference osisRef="John.5.27">Joh 5:27</reference>). This title is always associated with His coming again, because the kingdom that then awaits Him in that which belongs to Him as the Saviour of man, the Restorer of the lost inheritance. "Son of man" expresses His VISIBLE state formerly in his humiliation hereafter in His exaltation. He "comes to the Ancient of days" to be invested with the kingdom. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.110.2">Psa 110:2</reference>: "The Lord shall send the rod of thy strength (Messiah) out of Zion." This investiture was at His ascension "with the clouds of heaven" (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.9">Ac 1:9</reference>; 2:33, 34; <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6-Ps.2.9">Psa 2:6-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.18">Mt 28:18</reference>), which is a pledge of His return "in like manner" in the clouds" (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.11">Ac 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.64">Mt 26:64</reference>), and "with clouds" (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.7">Re 1:7</reference>). The kingdom then was given to Him in title and invisible exercise; at His second coming it shall be in visible administration. He will vindicate it from the misrule of those who received it to hold for and under God, but who ignored His supremacy. The Father will assert His right by the Son, the heir, who will hold it for Him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.27">Eze 1:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">He 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.13-Rev.19.16">Re 19:13-16</reference>). Tregelles thinks the investiture here immediately precedes Christ's coming forth; because He sits at God's right hand until His enemies are made His footstool, then the kingdom is given to the Son in actual investiture, and He comes to crush His so prepared footstool under His feet. But the words, "with the clouds," and the universal power actually, though invisibly, given Him then (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.20-Eph.1.22">Ep 1:20-22</reference>), agree best with His investiture at the ascension, which, in the prophetic view that overleaps the interval of ages, is the precursor of His coming visibly to reign; no event of equal moment taking place in the interval. <div eID="gen21899" type="x-p"/>
entries.e74564814ee239a8dbe1efc357bd47d3d24c1efa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12101"/><div sID="gen21900" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12101"/><hi type="bold">15. body--</hi>literally, "sheath": the body being the "sheath" of the soul. <div eID="gen21900" type="x-p"/>
entries.b13fa4fd591c4af04f69ec4869595d647abd04ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12102"/><div sID="gen21901" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12102"/><hi type="bold">17. kings--</hi>that is, kingdoms. Compare <reference osisRef="Dan.7.23">Da 7:23</reference>, "fourth kingdom"; <reference osisRef="Dan.2.38">Da 2:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.20-2Cor.8.22">8:20-22</reference>. Each of the four kings represents a dynasty. Nebuchadnezzar, Alexander, Antiochus, and Antichrist, though individually referred to, are representatives of characteristic tendencies. <div eID="gen21901" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffb7766121384928c9e0c1123eec57872ed9a015: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12103"/><div sID="gen21902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12103"/><hi type="bold">18. the Most High--</hi>the emphatic title of God in this prophecy, who delegates His power first to Israel; then to the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.37">Da 2:37</reference>, 38) when Israel fails to realize the idea of the theocracy; lastly, to Messiah, who shall rule truly for God, taking it from the Gentile world powers, whose history is one of continual degeneracy culminating in the last of the kings, Antichrist. Here, in the interpretation, "the saints," but in the vision (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Da 7:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">14</reference>), "the Son of man," takes the kingdom; for Christ and His people are one in suffering, and one in glory. Tregelles translates, "most high places" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Ep 1:3</reference>; 2:6). Though oppressed by the beast and little horn, they belong not to the earth from which the four beasts arise, but to the most high places. <div eID="gen21902" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fe50bd10f06831411e4558da55159a17299186e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12104"/><div sID="gen21903" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12104"/>19. Balaam, an Aramean, dwelling on the Euphrates, at the beginning of Israel's independent history, and Daniel at the close of it, prophetically exhibit to the hostile world powers Israel as triumphant over them at last, though the world powers of the East (Asshur) and the West (Chittim) carry all before them and afflict Eber (Israel) for a time (<reference osisRef="Num.23.8-Num.10.28">Nu 23:8-10, 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.24.2">24:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.24.7-Num.24.9">7-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.24.22-Num.24.24">22-24</reference>). To Balaam's "Asshur" correspond Daniel's two eastern kingdoms, Babylon and Medo-Persia; to "Chittim," the two western kingdoms, Greece and Rome (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.10.4">Ge 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.11.22">11, 22</reference>). In Babel, Nimrod the hunter (revolter) founds the first kingdom of the world (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.8-Gen.10.13">Ge 10:8-13</reference>). The Babylonian world power takes up the thread interrupted at the building of Babel, and the kingdom of Nimrod. As at Babel, so in Babylon the world is united against God; Babylon, the first world power, thus becomes the type of the God-opposed world. The fourth monarchy consummates the evil; it is "diverse" from the others only in its more unlimited universality. The three first were not in the full sense universal monarchies. The fourth is; so in it the God-opposed principle finds its full development. All history moves within the Romanic, Germanic, and Slavonic nations; it shall continue so to Christ's second advent. The fourth monarchy represents universalism externally; Christianity, internally. Rome is Babylon fully developed. It is the world power corresponding in contrast to Christianity, and therefore contemporary with it (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.38">Mt 13:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.1.15">Mr 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.1">Lu 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.4">Ga 4:4</reference>). <div eID="gen21903" type="x-p"/>
entries.d946e30d6266d0d7f7352f761e6f2858b2febf4c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12105"/><div sID="gen21904" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12105"/><hi type="bold">20. look ... more stout than ... fellows--</hi>namely, than that of the other horns. <div eID="gen21904" type="x-p"/>
entries.6dbdebf0f64b8a11a8455a72bb753b77ccd367ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12106"/><div sID="gen21905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12106"/><hi type="bold">21. made war with the saints--</hi>persecuted the Church (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.7">Re 11:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.7">13:7</reference>).<div eID="gen21905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prevailed--</hi>but not ultimately. The limit is marked by "until" (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.22">Da 7:22</reference>). The little horn continues, without intermission, to persecute up to Christ's second advent (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.12">Re 17:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.19">19:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.20">20</reference>). <div eID="gen21906" type="x-p"/>
entries.196b917fe7cd77960634fe5fd200667decba86e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12107"/><div sID="gen21907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12107"/><hi type="bold">22. Ancient of days came--</hi>The title applied to the Father in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Da 7:13</reference> is here applied to the Son; who is called "the everlasting Father" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>). The Father is never said to "come"; it is the Son who comes.<div eID="gen21907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment was given to ... saints--</hi>Judgment includes rule; "kingdom" in the end of this verse (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2">1Co 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Re 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.10">5:10</reference>; 20:4). Christ first receives "judgment" and the "kingdom," then the saints with Him (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Da 7:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">14</reference>). <div eID="gen21908" type="x-p"/>
entries.aef3dd722e2b9458b7148d2254fcb7becf4c09fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12108"/><div sID="gen21909" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12108"/><hi type="bold">24. ten horns--</hi>answering to the ten "toes" (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.41">Da 2:41</reference>).<div eID="gen21909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of this kingdom--</hi>It is out of the fourth kingdom that ten others arise, whatever exterior territory any of them possess (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.1">Re 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.12">17:12</reference>).<div eID="gen21910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rise after them--</hi>yet contemporaneous with them; the ten are contemporaries. Antichrist rises after their rise, at first "little" (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.8">Da 7:8</reference>); but after destroying three of the ten, he becomes greater than them all (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.20">Da 7:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.21">21</reference>). The three being gone, he is the eighth (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.17.11">Re 17:11</reference>); a distinct head, and yet "of the seven." As the previous world kingdoms had their representative heads (Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar; Persia, Cyrus; Greece, Alexander), so the fourth kingdom and its Antichrists shall have their evil concentrated in the one final Antichrist. As Antiochus Epiphanes, the Antichrist of the third kingdom in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.23-Dan.8.25">Da 8:23-25</reference>, was the personal enemy of God, so the final Antichrist of the fourth kingdom, his antitype. The Church has endured a pagan and a papal persecution; there remains for her an infidel persecution, general, purifying, and cementing [Cecil]. He will not merely, as Popery, substitute himself for Christ in Christ's name, but "deny the Father and the Son" (<reference osisRef="1John.2.22">1Jo 2:22</reference>). The persecution is to continue up to Christ's second coming (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.21">Da 7:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.22">22</reference>); the horn of blasphemy cannot therefore be past; for now there is almost a general cessation of persecution. <div eID="gen21911" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9aa59fdd2384cf07c1addd1ce1e958149948981: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12109"/><div sID="gen21912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12109"/>25. Three attributes of Antichrist are specified: (1) The highest worldly wisdom and civilization. (2) The uniting of the whole civilized world under his dominion. (3) Atheism, antitheism, and autotheism in its fullest development (<reference osisRef="1John.2.22">1Jo 2:22</reference>). Therefore, not only is power taken from the fourth beast, as in the case of the other three, but God destroys it and the world power in general by a final judgment. The present external Christianity is to give place to an almost universal apostasy.<div eID="gen21912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">think--</hi>literally, "carry within him as it were the burden of the thought."<div eID="gen21913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21914" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">change times--</hi>the prerogative of God alone (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.21">Da 2:21</reference>); blasphemously assumed by Antichrist. The "times and laws" here meant are those of religious ordinance; stated times of feasts [Maurer]. Perhaps there are included the times assigned by God to the duration of kingdoms. He shall set Himself above all that is called God (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference>), putting his own "will" above God's times and laws (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">Da 11:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.37">37</reference>). But the "times" of His wilfulness are limited for the elect's sake (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.22">Mt 24:22</reference>).<div eID="gen21914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they--</hi>the saints.<div eID="gen21915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21916" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given into his hand--</hi>to be persecuted.<div eID="gen21916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">time ... times and ... dividing of time--</hi>one year, two years, and half a year: 1260 days (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.6">Re 12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.14">14</reference>); forty-two months (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.2">Re 11:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.3">3</reference>). That literally three and a half years are to be the term of Antichrist's persecution is favored by <reference osisRef="Dan.4.16">Da 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.23">23</reference>, where the year-day theory would be impossible. If the Church, moreover, had been informed that 1260 years must elapse before the second advent, the attitude of expectancy which is inculcated (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.38">Lu 12:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">1Co 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.9">1Th 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.12">2Pe 3:12</reference>) on the ground of the uncertainty of the time, would be out of place. The original word for "time" denotes a stated period or set feast; or the interval from one set feast to its recurrence, that is, a year [Tregelles]; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.4">Le 23:4</reference>, "seasons"; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.44">Le 23:44</reference>, "feasts." The passages in favor of the year-day theory are <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.6">Eze 4:6</reference>, where each day of the forty during which Ezekiel lay on his right side is defined by God as meaning a year. Compare <reference osisRef="Num.14.34">Nu 14:34</reference>, where a year of wandering in the wilderness was appointed for each day of the forty during which the spies searched Canaan; but the days were, in these two cases, merely the type or reason for the years, which were announced as they were to be fulfilled. In the prophetic part of <reference osisRef="Num.14.34">Nu 14:34</reference> "years" are literal. If the year-day system was applied to them, they would be 14,400 years! In <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.4-Ezek.4.6">Eze 4:4-6</reference>, if day meant year, Ezekiel would have lain on his right side forty years! The context here in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.24">Da 7:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">25</reference>, is not symbolical. Antichrist is no longer called a horn, but a king subduing three out of ten kings (no longer horns, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.7">Da 7:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.8">8</reference>). So in <reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">Da 12:7</reference>, where "time, times, and half a time," again occurs, nothing symbolic occurs in the context. So that there is no reason why the three and a half years should be so. For the first four centuries the "days" were interpreted literally; a mystical meaning of the 1260 days then began. Walter Brute first suggested the year-day theory in the end of the fourteenth century. The seventy years of the Babylonian captivity foretold by Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">Jr 25:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">29:10</reference>) were understood by Daniel (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.2">Da 9:2</reference>) as literal years, not symbolical, which would have been 25,200 years! [Tregelles]. It is possible that the year-day and day-day theories are both true. The seven (symbolical) times of the Gentile monarchies (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.24">Le 26:24</reference>) during Israel's casting off will end in the seven years of Antichrist. The 1260 years of papal misrule in the name of Christ may be represented by three and a half years of open Antichristianity and persecution before the millennium. Witnessing churches may be succeeded by witnessing individuals, the former occupying the longer, the latter the shorter period (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.3">Re 11:3</reference>). The beginning of the 1260 years is by Elliott set at A.D. 529 or 533, when Justinian's edict acknowledged Pope John II to be head of the Church; by Luther, at 606, when Phocas confirmed Justinian's grant. But 752 is the most likely date, when the temporal dominion of the popes began by Pepin's grant to Stephen II (for Zachary, his predecessor's recognition of his title to France), confirmed by Charlemagne. For it was then first that the little horn plucked up three horns, and so became the prolongation of the fourth secular kingdom [Newton]. This would bring us down to about A.D. 2000, or the seventh thousand millenary from creation. But Clinton makes about 1862 the seventh millenary, which may favor the dating from A.D. 529. <div eID="gen21917" type="x-p"/>
entries.34bffc1cc55f8a9bffc148013b3e8bd42242f1b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12110"/><div sID="gen21918" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12110"/><hi type="bold">26. consume ... destroy--</hi>a twofold operation. Antichrist is to be gradually "consumed," as the Papacy has been consuming for four hundred years past, and especially of late years. He is also to be "destroyed" suddenly by Christ at His coming; the fully developed man of sin (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3">2Th 2:3</reference>) or false prophet making a last desperate effort in confederacy with the "beast" (<reference osisRef="Rev.16.13">Re 16:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.16">14, 16</reference>) or secular power of the Roman empire (some conjecture Louis Napoleon): destroyed at Armageddon in Palestine. <div eID="gen21918" type="x-p"/>
entries.52a7b2ad71cd1ddbb276213456c773250a0507f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12111"/><div sID="gen21919" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12111"/><hi type="bold">27. greatness of the kingdom under ... whole heaven--</hi>The power, which those several kingdoms had possessed, shall all be conferred on Messiah's kingdom. "Under ... heaven" shows it is a kingdom on earth, not in heaven.<div eID="gen21919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">people of ... saints of ... Most High--</hi>"the people of the saints," or "holy ones" (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.24">Da 8:24</reference>, Margin): the Jews, the people to whom the saints stand in a peculiar relation. The saints are gathered out of Jews and Gentiles, but the stock of the Church is Jewish (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.24">Ro 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.24">11:24</reference>); God's faithfulness to this election Church is thus virtually faithfulness to Israel, and a pledge of their future national blessing. Christ confirms this fact, while withholding the date (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.6">Ac 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen21920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21921" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting kingdom--</hi>If everlasting, how can the kingdom here refer to the millennial one? Answer: Daniel saw the whole time of future blessedness as one period. The clearer light of the New Testament distinguishes, in the whole period, the millennium and the time of the new heaven and new earth (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.20.4">Re 20:4</reference> with <reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">Re 21:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Rev.22.5">Re 22:5</reference>). Christ's kingdom is "everlasting." Not even the last judgment shall end it, but only give it a more glorious appearance, the new Jerusalem coming down from God out of heaven, with the throne of God and the Lamb in it (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.5.9">Re 5:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">11:15</reference>). <div eID="gen21921" type="x-p"/>
entries.74dacdf9f29319d0a1346cfd7b2472da762e81b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12112"/><div sID="gen21922" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12112"/><hi type="bold">28. cogitations ... troubled me--</hi>showing that the Holy Spirit intended much more to be understood by Daniel's words than Daniel himself understood. We are not to limit the significance of prophecies to what the prophets themselves understood (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1Pe 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>). <chapter eID="Dan.7"/>

entries.e9013766b8b8fe74442cbe287b651e3505a292a9: <div eID="gen33080" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33081" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33082" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33082" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33081" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33083" type="x-p"/> The prophet having, in the preceding chapters of this book, related some remarkable events concerning himself and his brethren in the captivity, and given proof of his being enabled, by Divine assistance, to interpret the dreams of others, enters now into a detail of his own visions, returning to a period prior to the transactions recorded in the last chapter. The first in order of the prophet's visions is that of the four beasts, which arose out of a very tempestuous ocean, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.1-Dan.7.9">Dan 7:1-9</reference>; and of one like the Son of man who annihilated the dominion of the fourth beast, because of the proud and blasphemous words of one of its horns, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.9-Dan.7.14">Dan 7:9-14</reference>. An angel deciphers the hieroglyphics contained in this chapter, declaring that the Four beasts, diverse one from another, represent the Four Paramount empires of the habitable globe, which should succeed each other; and are evidently the same which were shadowed forth to Nebuchadnezzar by another set of hieroglyphics, (see the second chapter), <reference osisRef="Dan.7.15-Dan.7.26">Dan 7:15-26</reference>. But for the consolation of the people of God, it is added that, at the time appointed in the counsel of Jehovah, "the kingdom and dominion, and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven, shall be given to the saints of the Most High;" and that this kingdom shall never be destroyed or transferred to another people, as all the preceding dominations have been, but shall itself stand for ever, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.27">Dan 7:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.28">Dan 7:28</reference>. It will be proper to remark that the period of a time, times, and a half, mentioned in the twenty-fifth verse as the duration of the dominion of the little horn that made war with the saints, (generally supposed to be a symbolical representation of the papal power), had most probably its commencement in a.d. 755 or 756, when Pepin, king of France, invested the pope with temporal power. This hypothesis will bring the conclusion of the period to about the year of Christ 2000, a time fixed by Jews and Christians for some remarkable revolution; when the world, as they suppose, will be renewed, the wicked cease from troubling the Church, and the saints of the Most High have dominion over the whole habitable globe. But this is all hypothesis. <div eID="gen33083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33084" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33085" type="x-p"/> In the first year of Belshazzar - This is the same Belshazzar who was slain at the taking of Babylon, as we have seen at the conclusion of chap. 5. That chapter should have followed both this and the succeeding. The reason why the fifth chapter was put in an improper place was, that all the historic parts might be together, and the prophetic be by themselves; and, accordingly, the former end with the preceding chapter, and the latter with this. The division therefore is not chronological but merely artificial. <div eID="gen33085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33086" type="x-p"/> Told the sum of the matters - That he might not forget this extraordinary dream, he wrote down the leading particulars when he arose.
entries.daede94eec5133da8de5055b8e83265e1c585624: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33087" type="x-p"/> The four winds of the heaven strove upon the great sea - The idea of strife is taken here from the effects that must be produced, were the east, the west, the north, and the south winds to rise tempestuously, and meet on the surface of the sea. By the great sea, the Mediterranean is meant; and is so called to distinguish it from those lakes called seas by the Hebrews; such as the Sea of Galilee, Dead Sea, Sea of Tiberias, etc.; but even that may refer to Asia, the scene of all these contentions. This dream is the same in meaning, under different emblems, as that of Nebuchadnezzar's metallic image; but in Daniel's dream several circumstances are added. It is supposed that Daniel had this dream about forty-eight years after Nebuchadnezzar had the vision of the great image.
entries.b4b5d503e51804c482aad80b04c79e9823a4c30e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33088" type="x-p"/> Four great beasts came up from the sea - The term sea, in Hebrew ים yam, from המה hamah, to be tumultuous, agitated, etc., seems to be used here to point out the then known terraqueous globe, because of its generally agitated state; and the four winds striving, point out those predatory wars that prevailed almost universally among men, from the days of Nimrod, the founder of the Assyrian or Babylonish monarchy, down to that time, and in the end gave birth to the four great monarchies which are the subject of this vision. <div eID="gen33088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33089" type="x-p"/> Diverse one from another - The people were different; the laws and customs different; and the administration of each differently executed.
entries.950b7fc1e42c56334e1e7bb5ae6ec9639bc2f28f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33090" type="x-p"/> The first was like a lion, and had eagle's wings - Bp. Newton well remarks, that these great beasts, as explained by the angel, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.17">Dan 7:17</reference>, are kingdoms. They arise out of a stormy and tempestuous sea; that is, out of the wars and commotions of the world; and they are called great in comparison of other states and kingdoms, and are denominated beasts for their tyrannical and cruel oppression. <div eID="gen33090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33091" type="x-p"/> These four beasts are indeed monstrous productions; a lion with eagle's wings; a bear with three ribs in its mouth; a leopard with four wings, and four heads; and a beast with ten horns. But such emblems and hieroglyphics were usual among the eastern nations, as may be seen in the monuments of antiquity. A winged lion, and such like fictitious animals, may be seen in many parts of the ruins of Persepolis. Horns are attributed to beasts which naturally have none, being used in hieroglyphic writings for symbols of strength and power. And such figures are supposed to be the symbols of different nations; and are not more strange than many that are still used in heraldry. I believe the science of heraldry arose out of the knowledge gained from the symbols used in the Sacred Writings, and the little acquaintance anciently obtained of the meaning of some of the Egyptian hieroglyphics. Hence our wiverons, griffins, unicorns, with a congeries of natural and unnatural things, split eagles, two-headed swans, etc., etc., etc. <div eID="gen33091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33092" type="x-p"/> The beast like a lion is the kingdom of the Babylonians; and the king of Babylon is compared to a lion, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.7">Jer 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.29">Isa 5:29</reference>; and is said to fly as an eagle, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jer 48:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.17.7">Eze 17:7</reference>. The lion is considered the king of the beasts, and the eagle the king of the birds; and therefore the kingdom of Babylon, which was signified by the golden head of the great image, was the first and noblest of all the kingdoms; and was the greatest then in being. The wings of the eagle denote the rapidity with which the lion - Nebuchadnezzar, made his conquests; for in a few years, by his own arms, he brought his empire to such an extent, and raised it to such a degree of eminence, as was truly surprising; and all tended to show with what propriety this eagle-winged lion is here made his emblem. <div eID="gen33092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33093" type="x-p"/> The wings thereof were plucked - Lydia, Media, and Persia, which had been provinces of the Babylonish empire, cast off the yoke, and put themselves under kings of their own. Besides, the rapidity of its conquests was stopped by its wars with the Medes and Persians; by whom it was at last conquered, and divided between Darius the Mede and Cyrus the Persian. <div eID="gen33093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33094" type="x-p"/> And it was lifted up from the earth - That is, the wings were plucked, rendered unfit for farther flight, by which it had before been lifted up from the earth; making its conquests almost with the rapidity of an eagle's flight. In what a short time did Nebuchadnezzar, who is here chiefly intended, conquer Syria, Phoenicia, Judea, Egypt, Arabia, etc.! But on his death the wings were plucked; and no farther extension of the empire took place under Evil-merodach or Belshazzar, till it was lost by the latter, and became divided as we have seen above. <div eID="gen33094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33095" type="x-p"/> And made stand upon the feet as a man - This I think refers to the taming of Nebuchadnezzar's pride. He had acted like a fierce and ravening lion. God struck him with insanity; he then lived the life of a beast, and had a beast's heart-disposition, and habits. At last God restored him. <div eID="gen33095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33096" type="x-p"/> And a man's heart was given to it - He became humane, humble, and pious; and in this state he appears to have died.
entries.7a51d08933c33b214a89e8c36f1c63781df81683: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33097" type="x-p"/> Another beast - like to a bear - This was the Medo-Persian empire, represented here under the symbol of the bear, as the largest species of these animals was found in Media, a mountainous, cold, and rough country, covered with woods. The Medes and Persians are compared to a bear on account of their cruelty and thirst after blood, a bear being a most voracious and cruel animal; the bear is termed by Aristotle an all-devouring animal; and the Medo-Persians are known to have been great robbers and spoilers. See <reference osisRef="Jer.51.48-Jer.51.56">Jer 51:48-56</reference>. The Persians were notorious for the cruelty of their punishments. See Calmet. <div eID="gen33097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33098" type="x-p"/> Raised up itself on one side - Cyrus arose on the borders of Chaldea, and thus the bear appeared to put itself in the position to attack the lion. <div eID="gen33098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33099" type="x-p"/> It had three ribs in the mouth of it - As if it had just finished its repast on some animal that it had seized. Some think three tusks curved like ribs, are meant; others three throats, עלעין illin, by which it (Cyrus) had absorbed the three empires of the Babylonians, Medes, and Persians; for these symbolic animals do not so much denote four empires, as four kings. See <reference osisRef="Jer.51.17">Jer 51:17</reference>. Others think three row of teeth are meant to denote the triple power of the Medes, Persians, and Babylonians, conjoined. Or the east, north, and south, which were subdued by the Persians. But the ribs being between the teeth of the bear may show how Babylon, Lydia, and Egypt were ground and oppressed by the bear - the Persians; though, as ribs strengthen the body, they were a powerful support to their conquerors.
entries.f8d1239b3dcbcaf2c03facb5995998a966130542: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen33099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33100" type="x-p"/> Another like a leopard - four wings - four heads - This was the Macedonian or Greek empire; and Alexander the Great its king. Alexander and his subjects are fitly compared to a leopard. <div eID="gen33100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33101" type="x-p"/> 1. The leopard is remarkable for its swiftness. Alexander and the Macedonians were very rapid in their conquests. <div eID="gen33101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33102" type="x-p"/> 2. The leopard is a spotted animal; a proper emblem of the various nations, with their various customs and languages, which constituted the Macedonian empire. It may refer to the character of Alexander himself, sometimes mild, at others cruel; sober and drunken; continent and lecherous; having a great power of self-government, and at other times being a slave to his passions. <div eID="gen33102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33103" type="x-p"/> 3. The leopard, though small, is not afraid to attack the lion. <div eID="gen33103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33104" type="x-p"/> Four wings of a fowl - The Babylonian empire was represented with two wings; and they sufficiently marked the rapidity of Nebuchadnezzar's conquests; but the Macedonian has here four wings; for nothing, in the history of the world, was equal to the conquests of Alexander, who ran through all the countries from Illyricum and the Adriatic Sea to the Indian Ocean and the River Ganges; and in twelve years subdued part of Europe, and all Asia. <div eID="gen33104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33105" type="x-p"/> The beast had also four heads - Signifying the empire after the death of Alexander, divided between his four generals. Cassander reigning over Macedon and Greece; Lysimachus, over Thrace and Bithynia; Ptolemy, over Egypt; and Seleucus, over Syria. <div eID="gen33105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33106" type="x-p"/> Dominion was given to it - It was not owing to the skill, courage, or valor of Alexander and his troops, that he made those wondrous conquests; the nations were given to him. For, as Bishop Newton says, had he not been assisted by the mighty power of God, how could he, with only thirty thousand men, have overcome Darius with six hundred thousand; and in so short a time have brought the countries from Greece as far as India into subjection?
entries.d8b7e5993e4f10ef44a19259f26f1e83aa517fcf: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33107" type="x-p"/> I saw - a fourth beast - it had great iron teeth - This is allowed, on all hands, to be the Roman empire. It was dreadful, terrible, and exceeding strong: it devoured, and brake in pieces, and stamped the residue, that is, the remains of the former kingdoms, with its feet. It reduced Macedon into a Roman province about one hundred and sixty-eight years before Christ; the kingdom of Pergamos about one hundred and thirty-three years; Syria about sixty-five; and Egypt about thirty years before Christ. And, besides the remains of the Macedonian empire, it subdued many other provinces and kingdoms; so that it might, by a very usual figure, be said to devour the whole earth, to tread it down, and break it to pieces; and became in effect, what the Roman writers delight to call it, the empire of the whole world. <div eID="gen33107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33108" type="x-p"/> It (the fourth beast) was diverse from all the beasts that were before it - Not only in its republican form of government, but also in power and greatness, extent of dominion, and length of duration. <div eID="gen33108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33109" type="x-p"/> It had ten horns - The ten kingdoms into which the Roman empire was afterwards divided. Calmet says, ten Syrian kings: and he finds them thus: - <div eID="gen33109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33110" type="x-p"/> 1. Seleucus Nicator. <div eID="gen33110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33111" type="x-p"/> 2. Antiochus Soter. <div eID="gen33111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33112" type="x-p"/> 3. Antiochus Theos. <div eID="gen33112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33113" type="x-p"/> 4. Antiochus Callinicus. <div eID="gen33113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33114" type="x-p"/> 5. Seleucus Ceraunus. <div eID="gen33114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33115" type="x-p"/> 6. Antiochus the Great. <div eID="gen33115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33116" type="x-p"/> 7. Seleucus, surnamed Philopater, brother of Antiochus Epiphanes. <div eID="gen33116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33117" type="x-p"/> 8. Laomedon of Mitylene, to whom Syria and Phoenicia had been intrusted. <div eID="gen33117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33118" type="x-p"/> 9. Antigone. And, <div eID="gen33118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33119" type="x-p"/> 10. His son Demetrius, who possessed those provinces, with the title of kings. <div eID="gen33119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33120" type="x-p"/> This is too much like forced work. There are different opinions concerning these ten kings; or rather which they were that constituted this division of the Roman empire. They are reckoned thus: - <div eID="gen33120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33121" type="x-p"/> 1. The Roman senate. <div eID="gen33121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33122" type="x-p"/> 2. The Greeks, in Ravenna. <div eID="gen33122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33123" type="x-p"/> 3. The Lombards in Lombardy. <div eID="gen33123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33124" type="x-p"/> 4. The Buns in Hungary. <div eID="gen33124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33125" type="x-p"/> 5. The Alemans, in Germany. <div eID="gen33125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33126" type="x-p"/> 6. The Franks in France. <div eID="gen33126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33127" type="x-p"/> 7. The Burgundians in Burgundy. <div eID="gen33127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33128" type="x-p"/> 8. The Saracens in Africa, and a part of Spain. <div eID="gen33128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33129" type="x-p"/> 9. The Goths, in other parts of Spain. <div eID="gen33129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33130" type="x-p"/> 10. And the Saxons, in Britain.
entries.37529540a16d9f08b963d3ec2937f8e64886a7ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen33130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33131" type="x-p"/> Another little horn - Among Protestant writers this is considered to be the popedom. <div eID="gen33131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33132" type="x-p"/> Before whom there were three of the first horns plucked up - These were probably, <div eID="gen33132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33133" type="x-p"/> 1. The exarchate of Ravenna. <div eID="gen33133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33134" type="x-p"/> 2. The kingdom of the Lombards. And, <div eID="gen33134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33135" type="x-p"/> 3. The state of Rome. <div eID="gen33135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33136" type="x-p"/> The first was given to the Pope, Stephen II., by Pepin, king of France, a.d. 755; and this constituted the pope's temporal princes. The second was given to St. Peter by Charlemagne, in 774. The third, the state of Rome, was vested in the pope, both in spirituals and temporals, and confirmed to him by Lewis the pious. These are the three horns which were plucked up from the roots before the little horn. <div eID="gen33136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33137" type="x-p"/> Were eyes like the eyes of a man - Intimating cunning and superintendence; for the pope calls himself Episcopus episcoporum, the Overseer of overseers. <div eID="gen33137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33138" type="x-p"/> And a mouth speaking great things - Full of boasting; pretending to unlimited jurisdiction; binding and loosing at pleasure; promising to absolve from all sins, present, past, and future; and threatening to send to everlasting destruction all kings, kingdoms, and individuals, who would dare to dispute his power and authority.
entries.a480c103feb1650c5b2750621390d48d95d4ed3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33139" type="x-p"/> The thrones were cast down - דמיו might be translated erected, so the Vulgate, positi sunt, and so all the versions; but that ours is a proper translation, is sufficiently evident from <reference osisRef="Dan.3.6">Dan 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.16">Dan 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.20">Dan 3:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.6.17">Dan 6:17</reference>, etc.; where the original word can be used in no other sense than that of throwing or casting down. There is a reference here to preparations made for a general assize, or to the convocation of the sanhedrin, where the father of the consistory sat with his assessors on each side in the form of a semicircle, and the people stood before them. <div eID="gen33139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33140" type="x-p"/> The Ancient of days - God Almighty; and this is the only place in the sacred writings where God the Father is represented in a human form.
entries.274a1091076a0e918b43cec831bd9ed866791773: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen33140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33141" type="x-p"/> A fiery stream issued - This is not spoken of the final judgment; but of that which he was to execute upon this fourth beast, the Roman empire; and the little boasting horn which is a part of the fourth beast, and must fall when the other falls.
entries.de64f5df4d10cb1ef81dd47116173020181a7244: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33142" type="x-p"/> I beheld then because of the voice (or, the beast will be destroyed because) of the great words which the horn spake - his body destroyed - When the dominion was taken from the rest of the beasts, their bodies were not destroyed, but suffered to continue still in being; but when the dominion shall be taken away from this beast, his body shall be totally destroyed; because other kingdoms succeeded to those, but no other earthly kingdom shall succeed to this. - Bishop Newton.
entries.cb1148a6233c7ef8c86cc77bb74f4e0e450fd9fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen33142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33143" type="x-p"/> One like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven - This most certainly points out the Lord Jesus, בר אנש bar enosh, the Son of miserable man; who took our nature upon him that he might redeem us unto himself. To prove himself to be the Messiah he applies, before the high priests, these words of the Prophet Daniel to himself <reference osisRef="Mat.24.30">Mat 24:30</reference>. <div eID="gen33143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33144" type="x-p"/> Near before him - The Ancient of days.
entries.10a5bffb203b114272ced1b7de5ed56b57a28a9a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen33144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33145" type="x-p"/> And there was given him dominion - This also is applied to our Lord Jesus by himself, after his resurrection, <reference osisRef="Mat.28.18">Mat 28:18</reference>. <div eID="gen33145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33146" type="x-p"/> His dominion is an everlasting dominion - Christianity shall increase, and prevail to the end of the world. See the parallel passages in the margin.
entries.25bd81022369e6e3b915dd8591453d55702536d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen33146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33147" type="x-p"/> I Daniel was grieved, etc. - The words in the original are uncommonly emphatic. My spirit was grieved, or sickened, בגו נדנה bego nidneh, within its sheath or scabbard. Which I think proves, <div eID="gen33147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33148" type="x-p"/> 1. That the human spirit is different from the body. <div eID="gen33148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33149" type="x-p"/> 2. That it has a proper subsistence independently of the body, which is only its sheath for a certain time. <div eID="gen33149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33150" type="x-p"/> 3. That the spirit may exist independently of its body, as the sword does independently of its sheath.
entries.6e3ffb28432a72dd89124e6fa39142302350f742: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen33150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33151" type="x-p"/> These great beasts - are four kings - See the preceding verses, where the following explanations are inserted and illustrated.
entries.136df2809e305ad4475d105bbe5a757d21bb8c13: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen33151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33152" type="x-p"/> But the saints of the Most High shall take the kingdom - I doubt whether this be the true sense of the original Chaldee, ויקבלון מלכותא קדשי עליונון vikabbelun malcutha kaddishey elyonin, "But the supreme holy ones shall receive the kingdom;" or, "they shall receive the kingdom of the supreme saints." Properly translated by Montanus, Et suscipient regnum sanctorum altissimorum. Whatever we may think of the patriarchs and the Jews in their best times, there has never been so much holiness of heart possessed, and so much righteousness practiced, as by the genuine disciples of Christ. Christianity alone has provided a full redemption for man. They are the chief saints, and to them God gives the kingdom: and this Gospel dispensation, called often the kingdom of God, and the kingdom of heaven, shall last for ever, during the whole lapse of time; and for ever and ever - throughout eternity, shall they and its blessings endure.
entries.42776d90fd07ac611c2cce19b30d8f50ce6b49d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen33152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33153" type="x-p"/> His nails of brass - This is not mentioned in the seventh verse, where the description of the beast is given. It might be added, for the first time, by the person who is now explaining the fourth beast. Houbigant thinks it has been lost out of the text: but such loss is not intimated by any MS.; nor does any of the ancient Versions acknowledge this addition in the seventh verse.
entries.f618729ec2731b28d893fc3f7ea3bb9f1e48866d: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen33153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33154" type="x-p"/> The same horn made war with the saints, and prevailed against them - Those who make Antiochus the little horn, make the saints the Jewish people. Those who understand the popedom by it, see this as referring to the cruel persecutions of the popes of Rome against the Waldenses and Albigenses, and the Protestant Church in general.
entries.ad7637f5dfd7f5ed98335b7427aada6bfd40eb99: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen33154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33155" type="x-p"/> Saints of the Most High - To the supereminent saints; see the note on <reference osisRef="Dan.7.18">Dan 7:18</reference> (note).
entries.f0720b47d0df1aa556b4e7edabd3810da9c9e89f: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen33155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33156" type="x-p"/> He shall speak great words against the Most High - Sermones quasi Deus loquetur; "He shall speak as if he were God." So St. Jerome quotes from Symmachus. To none can this apply so well or so fully as to the popes of Rome. They have assumed infallibility, which belongs only to God. They profess to forgive sins, which belongs only to God. They profess to open and shut heaven, which belongs only to God. They profess to be higher than all the kings of the earth, which belongs only to God. And they go beyond God in pretending to loose whole nations from their oath of allegiance to their kings, when such kings do not please them! And they go against God when they give indulgences for sin. This is the worst of all blasphemies! <div eID="gen33156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33157" type="x-p"/> And shall wear out the saints - By wars, crusades, massacres, inquisitions, and persecutions of all kinds. What in this way have they not done against all those who have protested against their innovations, and refused to submit to their idolatrous worship? Witness the exterminating crusades published against the Waldenses and Albinenses. Witness John Huss, and Jerome of Prague. Witness the Smithfield fires in England! Witness God and man against this bloody, persecuting, ruthless, and impure Church! <div eID="gen33157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33158" type="x-p"/> And think to change times and laws - Appointing fasts and feasts; canonizing persons whom he chooses to call saints; granting pardons and indulgences for sins; instituting new modes of worship utterly unknown to the Christian Church; new articles of faith; new rules of practice; and reversing, with pleasure, the laws both of God and man. - Dodd. <div eID="gen33158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33159" type="x-p"/> Until a time and times and the dividing of time - In prophetic language a time signifies a year; and a prophetic year has a year for each day. Three years and a half (a day standing for a year, as in <reference osisRef="Joh.9.24">Joh 9:24</reference>) will amount to one thousand two hundred and sixty years, if we reckon thirty days to each month, as the Jews do. <div eID="gen33159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33160" type="x-p"/> If we knew precisely when the papal power began to exert itself in the antichristian way, then we could at once fix the time of its destruction. The end is probably not very distant; it has already been grievously shaken by the French. In 1798 the French republican army under General Berthier took possession of the city of Rome, and entirely superseded the whole papal power. This was a deadly wound, though at present it appears to be healed; but it is but skinned over, and a dreadful cicatrice remains. The Jesuits, not Jesus, are now the Church's doctors. <div eID="gen33160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33161" type="x-p"/> If the papal power, as a horn or temporal power, be intended here, which is most likely, (and we know that that power was given in 755 to Pope Stephen II. by Pepin, king of France), counting one thousand two hundred and sixty years from that, we are brought to a.d. 2015, about one hundred and ninety years from the present [a.d. 1825]. But I neither lay stress upon nor draw conclusions from these dates. If the Church of Rome will reform itself, it will then be the true Christian Church, and will never be destroyed. Let it throw aside all that is ritually Jewish, all that is heathen; all that which pretends to be of God, and which is only of man, all doctrines that are not in the Bible; and all rites and ceremonies which are not of the appointment of Christ and his apostles; and then, all hail the once Roman, but now, after such a change, the Holy, Catholic Church! Every true Protestant would wish rather the reform than the extinction of this Church.
entries.3756d9db2044cb3cc7912c733579336bfaa9dbb3: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen33161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33162" type="x-p"/> The kingdom and dominion - The people of the saints of the Most High, or the people who are the supereminent saints, shall have the kingdom. Whatever name they may be distinguished by among men, these are the people, and theirs is the Church, that no lapse of time shall injure, and no power be able to destroy; but shall last as long as time shall endure.
entries.a40ba6ea4292f008c4c7297b2062caa5ae502017: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen33162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33163" type="x-p"/> The end of the matter - So said the expounding angel; and he said so because the purpose of God had determined it. In considering these things, and looking at the evils that shall come upon the world before those auspicious times can take place, I may say with Daniel, My cogitations much troubled me, and my countenance changed in me: but I keep the matter of my conjectures and consequent feelings in my own heart.  <chapter eID="Dan.7"/> <div eID="gen33163" type="x-p"/>

entries.cb48e401a756081374bb7869248391e5872f67f4: <div eID="gen15729" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Vision of the Four World-Kingdoms; the Judgment; and the Kingdom of the Holy God</title> <div sID="gen15730" type="x-p"/> After presenting to view (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.6">Daniel 3-6</reference>) in concrete delineation, partly in the prophetically significant experiences of Daniel and his friends, and partly in the typical events which befell the world-rulers, the position and conduct of the representatives of the world-power in relation to the worshippers of the living God, there follows in this chapter the record of a vision seen by Daniel in the first year of Belshazzar. In this vision the four world-monarchies which were shown to Nebuchadnezzar in a dream in the form of an image are represented under the symbol of beasts; and there is a further unfolding not only of the nature and character of the four successive world-kingdoms, but also of the everlasting kingdom of God established by the judgment of the world-kingdoms. With this vision, recorded like the preceding chapters in the Chaldean language, the first part of this work, treating of the development of the world-power in its four principal forms, is brought to a conclusion suitable to its form and contents. <div eID="gen15730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15731" type="x-p"/> This chapter is divided, according to its contents, into two equal portions. <reference osisRef="Dan.7.1-Dan.7.14">Dan 7:1-14</reference> contain the vision, and <reference osisRef="Dan.7.15-Dan.7.28">Dan 7:15-28</reference> its interpretation. After an historical introduction it is narrated how Daniel saw (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.2-Dan.7.8">Dan 7:2-8</reference>) four great beasts rise up one after another out of the storm-tossed sea; then the judgment of God against the fourth beast and the other beasts (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.9-Dan.7.12">Dan 7:9-12</reference>); and finally (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Dan 7:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Dan 7:14</reference>), the delivering up of the kingdom over all nations to the Son of man, who came with the clouds of heaven. Being deeply moved (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.15">Dan 7:15</reference>) by what he saw, the import of the vision is first made known to him in general by an angel (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.16-Dan.7.18">Dan 7:16-18</reference>), and then more particularly by the judgment (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.19-Dan.7.26">Dan 7:19-26</reference>) against the fourth beast, and its destruction, and by the setting up of the kingdom of the saints of the Most High (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.27">Dan 7:27</reference>). The narrative of the vision is brought to a close by a statement of the impression made by this divine revelation on the mind of the prophet (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.28">Dan 7:28</reference>).<note placement="foot">According to the modern critics, this vision also is to be regarded as belonging to the time of Antiochus Epiphanes; and, as von Lengerke says, the representation of the Messianic kingdom (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Dan 7:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Dan 7:14</reference>) is the only prophetic portion of it, all the other parts merely announcing what had already occurred. According to Hitzig, this dream-vision must have been composed (cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Dan 7:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.14">Dan 8:14</reference>) shortly before the consecration of the temple (1 Macc. 4:52, 59). On the other hand, Kranichfeld remarks, that if this chapter were composed during the time of the persecution under Antiochus Epiphanes, “then it would show that its author was in the greatest ignorance as to the principal historical dates of his own time;” and he adduces in illustration the date in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Dan 7:25</reference>, and the failure of the attempts of the opponents of its genuineness to authenticate in history the ten horns which grew up before the eleventh horn, and the three kingdoms (Dan 7:7., 20). According to <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Dan 7:25</reference>, the blaspheming of the Most High, the wearing out of the saints, and the changing of all religious ordinances continue for three and a half times, which are taken for three and a half years, after the expiry of which an end will be made, by means of the judgment, to the heathen oppression. But these three and a half years are not historically proved to be the period of the religious persecution under Antiochus Epiphanes. “In both of the books of the Maccabees (1 Macc. 1:54; 2 Macc. 10:5) the period of the desecration of the temple (according to v. Leng.) lasted only three years; and Josephus, <hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. xii. 7. 6, speaks also of <hi type="italic">three</hi> years, reckoning from the year 145 <hi type="italic">Seleucid</hi>. and the 25th day of the month Kisleu, when the first burnt-offering was offered on the idol-altar (1 Macc. 1:57), to the 25th day of Kisleu in the year 148 <hi type="italic">Seleucid</hi>., when for the first time sacrifice was offered (1 Macc. 4:52) on the newly erected altar.” But since the βδέλυγμα ἐρημώσεως was, according to 1 Macc. 1:54, erected on the 15th day of Kisleu in the year 145 <hi type="italic">Seleucid</hi>., ten days before the first offering of sacrifice upon it, most reckon from the 15th Kisleu, and thus make the period three years and ten days. Hitzig seeks to gain a quarter of a year more by going back in his reckoning to the arrival in Judea (1 Macc. 1:29, cf. 2 Macc. 5:24) of the chief collector of tribute sent by Apollonius. C. von Lengerke thinks that the period of three and a half years cannot be reckoned with historical accuracy. Hilgenfeld would reckon the commencement of this period from some other event in relation to the temple, which, however, has not been recorded in history. - From all this it is clear as noonday that the three and a half years are not historically identified, and thus that the Maccabean pseudo-Daniel was ignorant of the principal events of his time. Just as little are these critics able historically to identify the ten kings (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.7">Dan 7:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.7.20">Dan 7:20</reference>), as we shall show in an Excursus on the four world-kingdoms at the close of this chapter.</note> <div eID="gen15731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15732" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.1">Dan 7:1</reference> <div eID="gen15732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15733" type="x-p"/> The time here indicated, “in the first year of Belshazzar,” which cannot, as is evident, mean “shortly before the reign of Belshazzar” (Hitz.), but that Daniel received the following revelation in the course of the first year of the reign of this king, stands related to the contest of the revelation. This vision accords not only in many respects with the dream of Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 2), but has the same subject. This subject, however, the representation of the world-power in its principal forms, is differently given in the two chapters. In Daniel 2 it is represented according to its whole character as an image of a man whose different parts consist of different metals, and in Daniel 7 under the figure of four beasts which arise one after the other out of the sea. In the former its destruction is represented by a stone breaking the image in pieces, while in the latter it is effected by a solemn act of judgment. This further difference also is to be observed, that in this chapter, the first, but chiefly the fourth world-kingdom, in its development and relation to the people of God, is much more clearly exhibited than in Daniel 2. These differences have their principal reason in the difference of the recipients of the divine revelation: Nebuchadnezzar, the founder of the world-power, saw this power in its imposing greatness and glory; while Daniel, the prophet of God, saw it in its opposition to God in the form of ravenous beasts of prey. Nebuchadnezzar had his dream in the second year of his reign, when he had just founded his world-monarchy; while Daniel had his vision of the world-kingdoms and of the judgment against them in the first year of Belshazzar, i.e., Evilmerodach, the son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar, when with the death of the golden head of the world-monarchy its glory began to fade, and the spirit of its opposition to God became more manifest. This revelation was made to the prophet in a dream-vision by night upon his bed. Compare Dan 2:28. Immediately thereafter Daniel wrote down the principal parts of the dream, that it might be publicly proclaimed - <hi type="italic">the sum of the things</hi> (מלּין ראשׁ) which he had seen in the dream. אמר, <hi type="italic">to say, to relate</hi>, is not opposed to כּתב, <hi type="italic">to write</hi>, but explains it: by means of writing down the vision he said, i.e., reported, the chief contents of the dream, omitting secondary things, e.g., the minute description of the beasts.
entries.2c82557bc0306de50cbc38318ae0868534e559e9: <reference osisRef="Dan.7.2-Dan.7.3">Dan 7:2-3</reference> <div eID="gen15733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15734" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Dan.7.2">Dan 7:2</reference> Daniel begins his written report: “Daniel began and said,” introduces the matter. חזוי עם־ליליא, <hi type="italic">visions in </hi>(<hi type="italic">during</hi>)<hi type="italic">the night</hi>, cf. Dan 2:19. <reference osisRef="Dan.7.2">Dan 7:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.7.3">Dan 7:3</reference> describe the scene in general. The four winds of heaven break loose upon the great sea, and rage fiercely, so that four great beasts, each diverse from the others, arise out of its bosom. The great sea is not the Mediterranean (Berth., Ges., Hitz., Ewald), for such a geographical reference is foreign to the context. It is the ocean; and the storm on it represents the “tumults of the people,” commotions among the nations of the world (Häv., Leng., Hofm., etc.), corresponding to the prophetic comparison found in <reference osisRef="Jer.17.12">Jer 17:12</reference>; Jer 46:7. “Since the beasts represent the forms of the world-power, the sea must represent that out of which they arise, the whole heathen world” (Hofmann). In the interpretation of the image (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.17">Dan 7:17</reference>) יגּמא מן is explained by ארעא מן. גּיח means <hi type="italic">to break forth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.2">Eze 32:2</reference>), <hi type="italic">to burst out in storm</hi>, not causative, “to make the great sea break forth” (Kran.). The causative meaning is not certainly found either in the Hebrew or the Chaldee. The four winds stand in relation to the four quarters of the heavens; cf. Jer 49:39. Calvin remarks: <hi type="italic">Mundus similis turbulento mari, quod non agitatur una procella vel uno vento, sed diversis ventis inter se confligentibus, ac si totum coelum conspiraret ad motus excitandos</hi>. With this, however, the meaning of the words is not exhausted. The four winds of heaven are not merely <hi type="italic">diversi venti</hi>, and their bursting forth is not only an image of a general commotion represented by a storm in the ocean. The winds <hi type="italic">of the heavens</hi> represent the heavenly powers and forces by which God sets the nations of the world in motion; and the number four has a symbolical meaning: that the people of all regions of the earth are moved hither and thither in violent commotion. “(Ecumenical commotions give rise to oecumenical kingdoms” (Kliefoth). As a consequence of the storm on the sea, there arise out of it four fierce beasts, not all at once, but, as <reference osisRef="Dan.7.6">Dan 7:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.7.7">Dan 7:7</reference> teach, one after another, and each having a different appearance. The diversity of the form of the beasts, inasmuch as they represent kingdoms, is determined beforehand, not only to make it noticeable that the selection of this symbol is not arbitrary but is significant (Hävernick), but emphatically to intimate that the vision of different <hi type="italic">kingdoms</hi> is not to be dealt with, as many interpreters seem inclined to do, as one only of different <hi type="italic">kings</hi> of one kingdom.
entries.2849b190f45a04bedb4ebe3f40136fa59c4b8b44: <reference osisRef="Dan.7.4-Dan.7.8">Dan 7:4-8</reference> <hi type="italic">In these verses there is a description of the four beasts.</hi> - Dan 7:4. The first beasts resembled a lion with eagle’s wings. At the entrance to a temple at Birs Nimrud there has been found (Layard, <hi type="italic">Bab</hi>. and <hi type="italic">Nin</hi>.) such a symbolical figure, viz., a winged eagle with the head of a man. There have been found also images of winged beasts at Babylon (Münter, <hi type="italic">Relig. der Bab</hi>.). These discoveries may be referred to as evidence that this book was composed in Babylon, and also as explaining the Babylonian colouring of the dream. But the representation of nations and kingdoms by the images of beasts is much more widely spread, and affords the prophetic symbolism the necessary analogues and substrata for the vision. Lions and eagles are not taken into consideration here on account of their strength, rapacity, and swiftness, but simply because they are kings among beasts and birds: “The beast rules royally like the lion, and wings its conquering royal flight high over the οἰκουμένη like the eagle” (Kliefoth). This emblem corresponds with the representation of the first kingdom with the golden head (Daniel 2). What the gold is among metals and the head among the members of the body, that the lion is among beasts and the eagle among birds. <div eID="gen15734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15735" type="x-p"/> After a time Daniel sees a change take place with this beast. The wings, i.e., the feathers by which it flies, are plucked off: it is deprived of its power of flight, so that it can no more fly conquering over the earth, or hover as a ruler over it; i.e., the kingdom will be deprived of the power of conquering, for it will be lifted up from the earth (הקימת is Hoph., cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.4.33">Dan 4:33</reference>), and be placed on its feet as a man. The lifting up from the earth does not represent, accordingly, being taken away or blown away from the earth, not the destruction of the Chaldean kingdom (Theodrt., Hieron., Raschi, Hitzig, and others), but the raising of it up when lying prostrate on the ground to the right attitude of a human being. This change is further described by the words, “a man’s heart was given to it,” denoting that the beast-nature was transformed to that of a man. The three expressions thus convey the idea, that the lion, after it was deprived of its power of flight, was not only in external appearance raised from the form of a beast to that of a man, but also that inwardly the nature of the beast was ennobled into that of a man. In this description of the change that occurred to the lion there is without doubt a reference to what is said of Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4: it cannot, however, be thence concluded, with Hofmann and others, that the words refer directly to Nebuchadnezzar’s insanity; for here it is not the king, but the kingdom, that is the subject with reference to whose fate that event in the life of its founder was significant. Forasmuch as it was on account of his haughtiness that madness came upon him, so that he sank down to the level of the beasts of the field, so also for the same reason was his kingdom hindered in its flight over the earth. “Nebuchadnezzar’s madness was for his kingdom the plucking off of its wings;” and as when he gave glory to the Most High his reason returned to him, and then for the first time he attained to the true dignity of man, so also was his world-kingdom ennobled in him, although the continued influence of this ennobling may not be perceived from the events in the reign of his son, recorded in Daniel 5. Besides, there lies herein not only the idea of the superiority of the first world-kingdom over the others, as is represented in Daniel 2 by the golden head of the metallic image, but also manifestly the typical thought that the world-kingdom will first be raised to the dignity of manhood when its beast-like nature is taken away. Where this transformation does not take place, or where it is not permanent, there must the kingdom perish. This is the prophetic meaning, for the sake of which that occurrence in the life of the founder of the world-monarchy is here transferred to his kingdom.
entries.bdfdd99fac35a017f7c513932c7c1e82edf802ad: <reference osisRef="Dan.7.9-Dan.7.10">Dan 7:9-10</reference> <hi type="italic">The judgment on the horn speaking great things and on the other beasts, and the delivering of the kingdom to the Son of Man.</hi> <div eID="gen15738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15739" type="x-p"/> After Daniel had for a while contemplated the rising up of the little horn that appeared among the ten horns, the scene changed. There is a solemn sitting in judgment by God, and sentence is pronounced. Seats or chairs were placed. רמיו, <hi type="italic">activ</hi>. with an indefinite subject: <hi type="italic">they were thrown</hi>, i.e., they were placed in order quickly, or with a noise. Seats, not merely a throne for God the Judge, but a number of seats for the assembly sitting in judgment with God. That assembly consists neither of the elders of Israel (<hi type="italic">Rabb</hi>.), nor of glorified men (Hengstb. on <reference osisRef="Rev.4.4">Rev 4:4</reference>), but of angels (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.8">Psa 89:8</reference>), who are to be distinguished from the thousands and tens of thousands mentioned in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">Dan 7:10</reference>; for these do not sit upon thrones, but stand before God as servants to fulfil His commands and execute His judgments. יומין עתּיק, <hi type="italic">one advanced in days, very old</hi>, is not the Eternal; for although God is meant, yet Daniel does not see the everlasting God, but an old man, or a man of grey hairs, in whose majestic from God makes Himself visible (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.26">Eze 1:26</reference>). When Daniel represents the true God as an aged man, he does so not in contrast with the recent gods of the heathen which Antiochus Epiphanes wished to introduce, or specially with reference to new gods, as Hitzig and Kran. suppose, by reference to <reference osisRef="Deut.32.17">Deu 32:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.23.23">Jer 23:23</reference>; for God is not called the old God, but appears only as an old man, because age inspires veneration and conveys the impression of majesty. This impression is heightened by the robe with which He is covered, and by the appearance of the hair of His head, and also by the flames of fire which are seen to go forth from His throne. His robe is white as snow, and the hair of His head is white like pure wool; cf. Rev 1:14. Both are symbols of spotless purity and holiness. Flames of fire proceed from His throne as if it consisted of it, and the wheels of His throne scatter forth fire. One must not take the fire exclusively as a sign of punishment. Fire and the shining of fire are the constant phenomena of the manifestation of God in the world, as the earthly elements most fitting for the representation of the burning zeal with which the holy God not only punishes and destroys sinners, but also purifies and renders glorious His own people; see under Exo 3:3. The fire-scattering wheels of the throne show the omnipresence of the divine throne of judgment, the going of the judgment of God over the whole earth (Kliefoth). The fire which engirds with flame the throne of God pours itself forth as a stream from God into the world, consuming all that is sinful and hostile to God in the world, and rendering the people and kingdom of God glorious. קדמוהי מן (<hi type="italic">from before Him</hi>) refers to God, and not to His throne. A thousand times a thousand and ten thousand times ten thousand are hyperbolical expressions for an innumerable company of angels, who as His servants stand around God; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">Deu 33:2</reference>; Psa 68:18. The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> presents the Chaldaic form אלפין for the Hebraizing form of the text אלפים (<hi type="italic">thousands</hi>), and for רבון the Hebraizing form רבבן (<hi type="italic">myriads</hi>), often found in the Targg., to harmonize the plur. form with the singular רבּו going before. <div eID="gen15739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15740" type="x-p"/> Forthwith the judgment begins. יתב דּינא we translate, with most interpreters, <hi type="italic">the judgment sets itself</hi>. דּינא, <hi type="italic">judgment, abstr. pro concreto</hi>, as <hi type="italic">judicium</hi> in Cicero, <hi type="italic">Verr</hi>. 2. 18. This idea alone is admissible in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.26">Dan 7:26</reference>, and here also it is more simple than that defended by Dathe and Kran.: <hi type="italic">“</hi>He” (i.e., the Ancient of days) “sets Himself for judgment,” - which would form a pure tautology, since His placing Himself for judgment has been already (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.9">Dan 7:9</reference>) mentioned, and nothing would be said regarding the object for which the throne was set. - ”<hi type="italic">The books were opened.”</hi> The actions of men are recorded in the books, according to which they are judged, some being ordained to eternal life and others condemned to eternal death; cf. <reference osisRef="Rev.20.12">Rev 20:12</reference>, and the notes under Dan 12:1. The horn speaking great things is first visited with the sentence of death.
entries.f860492fff7c536e580d8227239b6c39f928d2ed: <reference osisRef="Dan.7.11">Dan 7:11</reference> <div eID="gen15740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15741" type="x-p"/> The construction of this verse is disputed. The second הוית חזה (<hi type="italic">I was seeing</hi>) repeats the first for the purpose of carrying on the line of thought broken by the interposed sentence. בּאדין (<hi type="italic">then</hi>) is separated by the accents from the first הוית חזה and joined to the clause following: <hi type="italic">“then on account of the voice of the great words.”</hi> By this interposed sentence the occasion of the judgment which Daniel sees passed upon the beast is once more brought to view. קל מן, <hi type="italic">“on account of the voice of the words,”</hi> i.e., on account of the loud words, not <hi type="italic">“</hi>from the time of the words, or from the time when the voice of the great words made itself heard” (Klief.). The following expression, דּי עד (<hi type="italic">till that</hi>), does not by any means require the temporal conception מן.
